The clear and undisputed champion of the game. Camden Brown had been putting things together throughout camp recently, and he really announced himself on Saturday night. CAMDEN BROWN!!!! pic.twitter.com/ayWtwHc2Y2 — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) August 16, 2026 CAAAAAMDEN BROOOOOOWN pic.twitter.com/44xjaS9O6n — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) August 16, 2026 Brown scored twice, the only touchdowns Dallas had, and the second one really was special. We say this all of the time around this time of year, but even if you don’t believe he deserves a spot on the final roster, him playing so well in such a loud fashion means that he is going to be difficult to stash on the practice squad if the team goes that direction. He feels safe. Stock Up: James Houston James Houston is not Jadeveon Clowney, but can Houston serve a similar role as the team’s cleanup guy on defense in the way that Clowney was last year? Saturday night made it seem possible. THAT’S JAMES HOUSTON pic.twitter.com/L6Nf6uXxLq — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) August 16, 2026 Unlike last year when the state of the pass rushers was flipped upside down a week before the season’s beginning, Houston does not have to be asked to be more than what he is. He can be someone who takes advantage of opportunities created by others. I see a player who checks that box. Do you? Stock Up: Marist Liufau The reality of Marist Liufau is that beauty is sort of in the eye of the beholder. The positional switch that the Cowboys have had him make under Christian Parker means we should take everything with a grain of salt, but he has found ways to be around positive action as of late (counting camp, obviously). Saturday offered more of that. Maybe it doesn’t wind up being enough and perhaps Liufau gets phased out because of roster math that doesn’t work in his favor. Right now though, there is no question that he is making the most of opportunities he is given and playing great overall team defense. Stock Up: Michael Trigg There was an early drop from Trigg that looked treacherous, but thankfully he wound up settling in and offered a stable presence in the passing game for the evening’s quarterbacks to work with. We all know that Jake Ferguson and Brevyn Spann-Ford are the team’s top two tight ends. The issue with Trigg becomes whether or not he can beat out Luke Schoonmaker for that TE3 spot as a fourth is not promised on the roster. The broadcast, the Cowboys version, sorry if you had the alternate, openly discussed how Schoonmaker playing in the game was a tough thing given his draft pedigree. Trigg hardly had the monstrous catches that we envisioned when the Cowboys signed him as an undrafted free agent, but it feels like he continues to offer more of “I’d rather buy that lottery ticket” than the alternative. Stock Up: Malik Davis If the Cowboys do have an RB2 right now it is certainly Malik Davis. It feels like Davis is the most trustworthy back in a world where a non-Javonte Williams has to have something like 16-18 carries. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but the Cowboys have clearly shown an effort to improve that spot on their roster. Sometimes players just refuse to let that happen, though. Malik Davis has been cut several times over, and he continues to come back and warrant a spot on the team. He is in the middle of that yet again. Stock Down: Caelen Carson If you did not see the game Caelen Carson had a rough outing early on. On the Seahawks’ first possession of the game, Carson was called for both pass interference and a facemask. This was the only drive of the game where Seattle scored, and it goes without saying that Carson’s penalties had a big impact in that regard. Carson also got called for holding soon after, and while he also had a nice PBU, the reality of this sort of thing is that those bad moments live and loom large. They cannot happen. This is an uphill battle at the moment. Stock Down: Anthony Smith It seemed throughout the second half like the Cowboys were trying to give Anthony Smith opportunities to capitalize and show out. They didn’t happen, but he wasn’t necessarily a big-time failure or anything. To be clear, this was the first professional game of Anthony Smith’s life. He was a seventh-round draft pick out of East Carolina just a few months ago and there is a steep lurning curve in the NFL. Sometimes that is the way things go. At the moment Smith seems like someone who could be a very viable practice squad candidate. There are still two preseason games to go, but nothing jumped out from him in this one. Stock Down: Traeshon Holden As noted with Caelen Carson, you absolutely do not want to make mistakes in preseason games. And as discussed throughout this conversation, there is a lot that goes into making a roster. Draft status matters. Money is a factor. The roster math is critical. For Traeshon Holden, Camden Brown is the talk o’ the town, Jonathan Mingo is getting some love, and Anthony Smith is a draft pick from this year. Holden has to do something to separate himself. Muffing a punt and giving the opposition a starting field position with five yards to go is not the way to do that. The Cowboys defense stood tall and kept the Seahawks from scoring which was a nice twist of fate, but that is certainly a moment that Holden wants back.
author: RJ Ochoa

title: Cowboys have interesting backup running back options
summary: The Dallas Cowboys found something safe with free agent Javonte Williams. The veteran showed up last year and delivered on all his upside attributes, from his physical running style to his reliability in pass protection. He was so dependable that it almost went unnoticed that the team didn’t have much of a backup running back […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Malik Davis #20 of the Dallas Cowboys runs with the ball during the third quarter during the NFL preseason game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys found something safe with free agent Javonte Williams. The veteran showed up last year and delivered on all his upside attributes, from his physical running style to his reliability in pass protection. He was so dependable that it almost went unnoticed that the team didn’t have much of a backup running back last year. The team re-upped on him this offseason, locking him down for the next three years, meaning the only thing left to be answered is who will be backing him up? The Cowboys are hoping that at least one of their second-year backs, Jaydon Blue or Phil Mafah, will emerge as a formidable option in the backfield. Blue brings the juice with his home run speed while Mafah is a power back that will plow through defenders. That seems like the plan anyway, but things don’t always go according to plan. Blue has shown some nice progress in camp. He’s making better decisions, and instead of just popping outside every chance he gets, he’s showing more discipline and hitting the inside gaps more regularly. He’s running hard, and when he finds space, he’s making explosive plays in practice. In practice. While that’s the good stuff, Blue has also made some mistakes. He’s put the ball on the ground multiple times, displaying poor ball security, and nothing will get you off the field quicker than turning over the ball. And his explosiveness in practice isn’t translating to live action as he struggled to find creases in Saturday’s preseason game against Seattle. He hit the hole hard, but he just drove himself into a wall, sometimes created by his own blockers. Blue just hasn’t been able to be that guy in space because he hasn’t been able to get into space. And then there’s Mafah. Like his teammate, he’s also looked good in camp. He’s been his usual bruising self, showing a lot of improvement in pass protection by standing firm and picking up blitzes. He’s catching balls out of the backfield, and keeps the ball well protected. Those things have looked nice in practice, but like Blue, he’s also struggled to find his footing in live action. If things are congested, he can’t cut his way out of it and will get stuck in the backfield. Against the Seahawks, Mafah was met early in the backfield and could never gain any traction. And while he offers better ball security, he’s falling victim to another one of his deficiencies. His durability. He suffered a chest injury early in the second half and was ruled out the rest of the game. Despite impressing in practice, these young backs didn’t do much to make the team feel like they can be the RB2 behind Williams. But one running back did. The forgotten one. Malik Davis. It’s crazy because every year, Davis shows up in Dallas, does well, but he’s always passed up for a back who offers much more upside, even if they’re not outperforming him in camp. He’s been cut multiple times, and many expect it to happen once again. Not so fast. When Davis entered the game on Saturday, the running game immediately got better. He didn’t break off any explosive runs or power through defenders, but instead, he did what he does best. He read his blocks, planted his foot in the turf, and took off. That’s it. There’s not much else to it. Just that little shuffle in his feet while retaining his speed, allowing him to burst through a small crease, is all he needed to turn a bad run into an efficient one. Davis was the team’s leading rusher on Saturday, averaging 5.6 yards per carry. Some may have forgotten that Davis was the team’s second-leading rusher last year behind Williams. Like Williams, he averaged an efficient 4.8 yards per carry as compared to 3.4 ypc from Blue and 3.6 ypc from Mafah. Signs are hinting that Davis once again becomes a fail-safe option for the Cowboys should it come to that. And despite many hoping that one of last year’s rookies would impress, that offers no guarantees. It’s possible that one, maybe both, do not improve enough to surprise the high-floor, but low-upside that Davis currently offers. This isn’t what fans want. Blue is supposed to be the guy who takes the top off the defense. Mafah is supposed to be the punisher. And while Davis doesn’t have those appealing traits to be a star, he has shown that he has the mental capacity and the physical ability to be an extension of an efficient running game Williams offers. There’s still time, and the Cowboys will still try to get one of these rookies to stick, but if it doesn’t happen, they know that they can once again rely on Davis to step in and get the job done.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Camden Brown leads scoring in strong defensive effort for Cowboys win at Seahawks
summary: The Dallas Cowboys were officially back on the field for the first time in 2026 on Saturday, and so too were the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. There were certainly some moments that reminded us all this is just the first appetizer towards the main course of week one regular season football. The Cowboys […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Israel Abanikanda (30) carries the ball against the Seattle Seahawks during the second half at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Steven Bisig-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys were officially back on the field for the first time in 2026 on Saturday, and so too were the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. There were certainly some moments that reminded us all this is just the first appetizer towards the main course of week one regular season football. The Cowboys won this appetizer of a game 17-7, falling behind 7-0 after the Seahawks went down the field with a 13-play scoring drive that proved to be their biggest offensive highlight of the night. The Cowboys were the only team to score the rest of the game, with 14 of these points coming on insane highlight reel catches for touchdowns by UDFA wide receiver Camden Brown, one from Sam Howell and one from Joe Milton. As we’ll do after every single Cowboys contest this season, let’s get to a few scouting notes on everything that went down between the Cowboys and Seahawks on Saturday night at Lumen Field. On Dallas’ first defensive possession to start the game, Caelen Carson and Shavon Revel Jr. were the two outside cornerbacks. Revel is technically a carryover from the failed Matt Eberflus defensive experiment of a year ago, but with so much missed time, he is primed to take to the coaching of Christian Parker and be the latest cornerback that takes leaps and strides under his secondary-focused coaching. On the other hand, Carson is a carryover going all the way back to Mike Zimmer’s defense in 2024, has not made as much noise at training camp, and it showed in this Seahawks game how making yet another coaching adjustment with multiple schemes already behind him is proving difficult for the former fifth-round pick. As a duo though, Carson and Revel combined to show what should be one of the overall strengths of Parker’s defensive game planning, and that is the flexibility to put individual players in the best position to win. On the very first snap of the game, Carson was in more of an off-coverage position compared to Revel being in press, and it helped Carson have the angle to make a strong tackle against the run towards the boundary. One play later, the Seahawks dropped back to pass for the first time, and targeted Revel – still in this press technique – who nearly intercepted the Drew Lock attempt. Unfortunately, one of the things that even good coaching and great individual plays can’t overcome on defense is free yards awarded to an offense, and that ended up being more of the story of the night for Carson. Two third-down penalties, first pass interference then a facemask, extended Seattle’s opening touchdown drive, and Carson had a third holding penalty later in the night. The Cowboys had strung together some good practice runs on offense in the red zone, but settled for a field goal on their first trip against the Seahawks. The big plays on the drive were a 13-yard screen pass to Jaydon Blue to get it started and two third-down conversions by Jonathan Mingo. Dallas went back to the screen to Blue in the red zone and it was not as effective, leading to the Brandon Aubrey 29-yard field goal. When it comes to Blue and Mingo, both provided insight into the roster battles at running back and wide receiver respectively with their play. Blue led the team in carries with eight, but gained just 19 yards with a long of four on these eight attempts compared to 39 yards on seven rushes for Malik Davis and 36 yards on the same number of attempts by Israel Abanikanda. Mafah ended the night with four carries for nine yards and was ruled out for futehr action after suffering a chest injury. The eye candy when it comes to all of the ways the Cowboys can use Blue is tempting, but his considerable lack of juice between the tackles compared to everyone else in the backfield right now is glaring as well. Many Cowboys fans have wanted Blue to gain the edge in the RB2 competition behind Javonte Williams because Williams is already that reliable power option between the tackles, but time and time again the offense is proving they work best when committing to those types of runs even more – even without Williams on the field. Davis and Abanikanda ran hard on the interior, with Davis having the longest run of the night for 14 yards. Both of these teams ran for the same 3.8 yards per carry in aggregate on the night, but the Cowboys running 11 more total plays with an over five minute advantage in time of possession and outrushing the Seahawks 137-107 tells the story of how they reclaimed control of the game and got a preseason opening win for the first time in a long time . The Cowboys using their experienced offensive line depth to run the ball physically was the difference here. As for Mingo and the WR battles, the star of the night at this position was easily UDFA Camden Brown. He made waves twice for circus catch touchdowns that will be played on every highlight show all week. On the first touchdown from Sam Howell, Brown was running a one-man route to his side of the field with safety help over the top, and still beat both defenders to the catch point and held on through contract and traffic to put Dallas ahead 10-7. The other touchdown was thrown by Joe Milton, a fade pass that Brown tracked towards the back pylon and could only get one hand on, but held on and got the feet in for another eye-popping score. Brown should easily be the favorite of the dark-horse receivers at this point to make the team. The best news from his performance is he was part of a bigger picture in the pass game that showed how efficient the Cowboys can be controlling games with their offense on the field. Brian Schottenheimer’s team did so while keeping things perfectly vanilla enough to not show the Seahawks (a team they’ll see again) any tips either. The Brown short yardage score was also made possible by UDFA TE Michael Trigg having two of his four catches on that drive, another big target in the pass game that can help the Cowboys be a physically imposing offense even through the air. Trigg came into this game having stacked some good practices together, and was able to keep some of that momentum going in Seattle. If it was undeniable that Camden Brown made the highlights of the night for the Cowboys offense, the lasting defensive highlights were a joint effort that came immediately after the lowlight of the whole night for Dallas, a special teams gaffe with Traeshon Holden muffing a punt to give the Seahawks first-and-goal at the five in the fourth quarter. Christian Parker’s defense came up with a goal line stand in the sudden change situation. On first down, Reddy Steward made a strong stop on the outside run to keep the Seahawks out of the endzone. The Seahawks tried the same corner of the endzone on second down with the outside run, and another secondary player, Julius Wood, made a difficult tackle to keep Seattle out of the endzone. Trying the interior instead on third down, the Cowboys defense again held up and brought up fourth down. On fourth and goal from the five, for the second time in the series, Tyrus Wheat got quick pressure off the edge and nearly sacked the quarterback, doing enough to allow Isaiah Land to finish the sack and make the stop. This was an awesome test for the Cowboys defense to be able to pass in their first preseason game, but overall their work on the night did raise some questions as well – primarily how this team will be able to consistently set a hard edge. Tyrus Wheat, James Houston, and Marist Liufau all showed some juice off the edge in pass rush, but especially Liufau also had his struggles staying square to the line of scrimmage and setting that hard edge, especially against the run. Dallas was obviously missing Kenny Clark, Quinnen Williams, and Otito Ogbonnia at defensive tackle.…
author: Sean Martin

title: 10 thoughts on the Cowboys 17-7 preseason win over the Seahawks
summary: Football finally happened. The Dallas Cowboys just completed their first preseason game with a 17-7 win over the Seattle Seahawks. It was great to see them in action after such a long hiatus from football, with lots of fun stuff to talk about. With this first game officially in the books, here are 10 thoughts […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; Dallas Cowboys quarterback Sam Howell (16) passes the ball against the Seattle Seahawks during the first half at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Steven Bisig-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Football finally happened. The Dallas Cowboys just completed their first preseason game with a 17-7 win over the Seattle Seahawks. It was great to see them in action after such a long hiatus from football, with lots of fun stuff to talk about. With this first game officially in the books, here are 10 thoughts on Saturday’s action. 1. Not a good start The preseason did not start out all that great as the defense allowed the Seahawks’ offense to stroll down the field for an opening drive touchdown. The cornerbacks got tagged not once, not twice, but three times for penalties when Caelen Carson and Twikweze Bridges both were flagged for pass interference. Carson also added a facemask penalty on the same drive. The Cowboys’ offense did not return the favor as they went three-and-out on their opening drive. It didn’t look good at first. 2. Things got better After stumbling early, the team rebounded nicely. The defense made stops, and the offense started scoring. The Cowboys went on a 17-0 run, seizing control of the game and never looking back. It was nice to see players showing more discipline as the game went on and coming up with plays. It was especially satisfying to see the defense respond the way it did. After surrendering 80 yards on the Seahawks’ opening drive, the Cowboys defense only gave up 76 yards total the rest of the game. That’s how you adjust. 3. Houston is a problem Last year, James Houston put himself on notice during the preseason when he made big play after big play. Well, he’s at it again. The veteran edge rusher came through with some plays, including two sacks (although one wasn’t officially counted due to an accepted penalty on the Seahawks), Thanks to his relentless motor, he’s just a guy who doesn’t quit, and when things start to break down, he finds the quarterback. 4. Howell draws first blood The veteran Sam Howell got the nod to start over Joe Milton III, and he was solid. He played the short game, mostly dumping off passes. He had a couple of nice slant passes to Jonathan Mingo. He made quick decisions and never made any mistakes, including holding the ball too long. He was never sacked. Howell only made one big throw, and that was a 39-yard touchdown pass to rookie UDFA Camden Brown. It wasn’t flashy, but it was efficient. Speaking of Brown… 5. What can Brown do for you? Every year, there’s an undrafted free agent wideout that catches everyone’s attention in training camp. You can set your watch to it. This year’s gem is Camden Brown. The rookie receiver has been dazzling with some nice catches, but he followed that up nicely with a great debut. He hauled in three catches for 62 yards, including two touchdowns. And both touchdowns were impressive catches, first coming back and winning a jump ball and then second with a great one-handed catch on a fade in the end zone. Hype happens, but often fades. Brown is keeping his roster-fighting chance rolling. 6. The second-half backs All eyes were on second-year running backs Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah with the hope that at least one of them would shine. They didn’t. The longest run of each player was just four yards. Blue finished with 19 yards on eight carries (2.4 ypc), and Mafah finished with nine yards on four carries (2.3 ypc). As bad as things were for those guys, the second-half backs looked much better. Both Malik Davis and Israel Abanikanda rushed for over five yards a carry as Davis finished with 39 yards on seven carries (5.6 ypc) while Abanikanda finished with 37 yards on seven carries (5.1 ypc). It’s hard to know for sure without looking at the tape, but the second-half guys seemed to do a better job reading the rushing lanes, hitting the holes quickly, and pushing forward. This battle should be interesting going forward, and quite honestly, the RB2 job is firmly up for grabs. 7. Milton answers back The team’s two backup options are contrasting players, as the younger Milton offers the team a little more big-play ability thanks to his legs and big arm. However, the problem for him has been his accuracy. In this game, the third-year quarterback looked much better. He did a good job staying in the pocket, making good decisions, and throwing strikes. The Cowboys coaches had a difficult choice entering this game, and it hasn’t gotten much easier after the game. 8. The protection held up There were some mental mishaps from the backup offensive line, but for the most part, they had a good showing. As mentioned before, the run game improved in the second half, and neither of the Cowboys’ quarterbacks was sacked. There is still a lot to sort out when it comes to figuring which guys make the final 53, but the interior looked pretty decent, giving them something to build on. 9. The not-so special teams It was a rough day for Nick Sorensen’s group as the special teams were horrid. In the first half, they gave up a 52-yard punt return. Then, in the second half, Traeshon Holden got caught in no-man’s land and tried to scoop up the ball near the goal line, only to not come up with it cleanly, resulting in a muffed recovery, turning the ball over to the Seahawks. 10. Goal line stand One good thing about the punt return miscue is that it set up a nice opportunity for the Cowboys defense to make a stand. With 1st-and-goal at the five-yard-line, the defense stood their ground with a nice sideline chase-down by safety Julius Wood, and was finished off with a fourth-down sack by Isaiah Land.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys news: Dallas win contains a lot of good, but also some issues
summary: The Dallas Cowboys played their first preseason game of the 2026 season and got a win versus the Seattle Seahawks. It didn’t start well for Dallas who gave up a quick TD, but they dominated the rest of the game. Training camp star Camden Brown carried his momentum into the game with two eye-popping touchdown […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Camden Brown #6 of the Dallas Cowboys reacts during the second quarter of the NFL preseason game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys played their first preseason game of the 2026 season and got a win versus the Seattle Seahawks. It didn’t start well for Dallas who gave up a quick TD, but they dominated the rest of the game. Training camp star Camden Brown carried his momentum into the game with two eye-popping touchdown catches. The Cowboys defense stiffened up, but the Dallas special teams still have work to do. Game Recap: Cowboys defeat Seattle, 17-7 – DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys started slow on defense, but made up for it the rest of the game. With backups largely playing in the first preseason game of the 2026 exhibition schedule, judging just how good new defensive coordinator Christian Parker’s defense is going to be is a bit tough. But after a slow start, his unit showed signs that things indeed might be different this year as it anchored the Dallas Cowboys to a 17-7 victory over the Seattle Seahawks. The unit gave up a touchdown on Seattle’s opening drive of the game, but took care of business over the rest of the night, which included a goal-line stand in the fourth that essentially sealed the game. As a group, they didn’t allow a point over the final three-and-a-half quarters and limited the Seahawks to just 156 total yards of offense and a measly 76 yards passing. Camden Brown stands out for Cowboys with 2 touchdown catches in 17-7 preseason win against Seahawks – AP via ESPN UDFA WR Camden Brown didn’t stop with practices, he showed up when the lights came on. Rookie Camden Brown had two touchdown catches, including a diving, one-handed snag, to help lead the Dallas Cowboys past the Seattle Seahawks 17-7 in the teams’ preseason opener Saturday night. Brown caught a 39-yard pass from Sam Howell in the second quarter to put Dallas up 10-7. On the first drive of the third quarter, Brown snared a fade pass from Joe Milton in the back left corner of the end zone for a 2-yard touchdown. Preseason Week 1: Cowboys settle into groove, shut down Seahawks, 17-7 – K.D. Drummond, Cowboys wire Special teams is still an issue under Nick Sorenson. There didn’t seem to be any improvement on last year. The special teams needs plenty of work yet again, as Nick Sorensen’s second season isn’t inspiring much hope out the gate. But with the fact that the starters weren’t suiting up, one hopes that the players who messed up in allowing the 52-yard punt return and then botched their own return at the goal line, will be nowhere near those roles in games that actually matter. Cowboys vs. Seahawks highlights | Preseason Week 1 – NFL.com In case you missed the game, you can see some of the highlights. Highlights from the Preseason Week 1 matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and the Seattle Seahawks during the 2026 NFL season. What We Learned About the Dallas Cowboys: Legitimate concerns emerge from preseason win, and roster moves could soon follow – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z sports We got some clues in the tight end battle for the Cowboys. Based on who played and who didn’t, we got a significant answer at tight end. Brevy Spann-Ford did not suit up Saturday, which tells us the Cowboys know he’s their No. 2 tight end and Jake Ferguson’s running mate in the offense. That clarity, however, opens a lot of question marks about former second-round pick Luke Schoonmaker, who got the start Saturday night. When Schoonmaker was taken out, he watched Michael Trigg haul in four catches for 30 yards in impressive fashion. Schoonmaker should be at least a little concerned about his roster spot. We’ll see how that evolves during the next two preseason games. Top Seahawks takeaways from 17-7 presason Week 1 loss to Cowboys – Dom Skene, Seahawks Wire A view of the game from the enemy’s point of view. While the rather excellent episode two of Hard Knocks has been the talk of the town the past week, the tape will reflect the team’s focus on managing and controlling violence. Derick Hall was coaching up Jalan Gaines, who was relentlessly attacking Dallas’ quarterbacks, and Mason Richman and Beau Stephens were taking the competition to the Dallas’ defensive line, both getting great downhill push in the run game. The young offensive lineman are a product of the culture Mike Macdonald and company have created and prioritized. Daily discussion question: What did you make of Saturday night’s game?
author: David Halprin

title: Stock Up, Stock Down after the Broncos’ preseason victory over the Falcons
summary: The Broncos have completed all but a handful of their training camp practices and have started the preseason with a dominant 27-7 victory over the Atlanta Falcons. So, the push towards the regular season is in full swing, and it is a good time to take a look at which players on the Broncos’ 90-man […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Denver wide receiver Courtland Sutton (14) reacts during the NFL pre-season game between the Denver Broncos and the Atlanta Falcons on August 14th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Broncos have completed all but a handful of their training camp practices and have started the preseason with a dominant 27-7 victory over the Atlanta Falcons. So, the push towards the regular season is in full swing, and it is a good time to take a look at which players on the Broncos’ 90-man roster are rising and fading as we get closer to Week 1. I am going to go through the Broncos’ entire 90-man roster by positional group and tell you if I believe a player’s stock is rising, falling, or remains unchanged, and give you my thoughts on their future with the team. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock up: Bo is back and healthy and looks good as new. His ankle looks fully healed from offseason surgery, and he has been moving around and running well at Broncos Camp. Everything is trending up for the Broncos’ starting quarterback, who will make his preseason debut this week. Jarrett Stidham – Stock up, slightly: There was talk that Stidham would be competing with Sam Ehlinger for the Broncos’ backup quarterback job. The two have been splitting second-team reps, but on Friday Night, Stiddy had a statement performance that may have all but ended the backup quarterback competition talk. Sam Ehlinger – Stock down, slightly: Heading into the game, he was in the QB2 conversation, but after Stidham’s performance, I believe that talk is all but dead. Ehlinger played alright, but was with the third-team offense, so it was hard to compare. He may get a shot with the second team this Friday, but simply due to Stidham’s performance, Ehlinger’s stock is down slightly. Running Back JK Dobbins – Unchanged: Sure, the veteran back is dealing with what seems like a minor soft tissue injury, but nothing has really changed here for Dobbins. He likely won’t play much, if at all, during the preseason, and he simply needs to be 100% for Week 1 vs. the Chiefs. RJ Harvey – Stock down/up: Harvey’s stock as a running back is down. His vision isn’t great, and he looks like the Broncos third best back behind Dobbins and rookie Jonah Coleman. However, Harvey’s stock as a pass catcher/weapon in space is up. I think he will be a pass-catching threat for the Broncos, who will get some carries, but most of his damage will be done in space. Jonah Coleman – Stock up: Coleman has been as advertised. A well-rounded back with great vision, power, soft hands, and can pass block. We saw his running ability on display vs. the Falcons, and I would not be surprised if Coleman starts the season as the Broncos’ RB2. Split time with Dobbins as the main ball carrier, while Harvey is your third down/pass catching specialist. Jaleel McLaughlin – Stock down: The number one thing you cannot do as a ball carrier is fumble, and that’s exactly what McLaughlin did vs. the Falcons. Otherwise, he looked like the back we have seen for the past few seasons. He’s on the roster bubble, and a fumble could put him in the doghouse and potentially on the hot seat for a roster spot. Tyler Badie – Unchanged: He kinda is who he is. He doesn’t offer a ton as a runner or pass catcher, but he earned the trust of the Broncos coaches and quarterback Bo Nix for his ability to pass block. That trust and skill could land him a spot on the practice squad this season. Cody Schrader – Unchanged: I liked how Schrader ran the ball, but he was playing behind the third-string OL, so it was a tough evaluation. Realistically, he’s competing for a spot on the practice squad, and I didn’t see much to warrant his stock to rise or drop after Friday’s game. Adam Prentice – Stock up: The Broncos fullback was used in key short-yardage situations and at the one-yard line, where he ran it in for a touchdown. He’s a favorite of the coaching staff and will be part of this team and this offense this upcoming season. Wide Receiver Courtland Sutton – Stock up: Load management seems to be paying off for the veteran wide receiver. He caught a 40-yard bomb in the first drive from Stidham and then made a highlight-reel one-handed catch and looked to be in midseason form. Jaylen Waddle – Stock up: He has been sidelined for about a week with a soft tissue injury, but the Broncos star receiver has shown enough before the injury for me to say stock up. He was practically unguardable during camp and showcased his speed and explosiveness throughout, and will be a big part of the Broncos’ success this upcoming season. Pat Bryant – Stock WAY up: Pat Bryant has been the story of camp thus far. The second-year wide receiver has been making plays throughout camp, has earned praise from the coaches and his teammates, and was featured early on vs. the Falcons. He has run away with the WR3 job and could be a productive member of this offense this upcoming season. Marvin Mims Jr. – Unchanged: I don’t believe we will see his role change much this upcoming season. He will be an All-Pro-caliber returner while getting snaps as an occasional deep threat/space player on offense. They can get creative with Mims, and I am excited to see how Davis Webb utilizes him. Troy Franklin – Stock down: It has to be down, right? Bryant seems to have taken the WR3 role, Mims has proven to be a better deep/speed threat throughout his career, and Franklin really hasn’t done much to move the needle thus far this summer. He did have a nice catch vs. the Falcons, but I have a hard time figuring out his exact role on this team outside of being a depth player. Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Stock up: As long as Sean Payton is coaching this team, LJH’s stock will be up. He is a reliable backup who gives you snaps at wide receiver, blocks well, and plays special teams. He may not make the 53-man roster, but he has a better shot at being active on game days than Troy Franklin right now. Michael Bandy – Slightly up: The Broncos like the Bandy man. He has been sidelined a little bit, but he has served as veteran depth the past few seasons, and until someone can surpass him, I think he will have the same role this season. Hakeem Butler – Stock slightly down: The former UFL standout has not made the impression that I anticipated and was mostly quiet vs. the Falcons. He will need to show more moving forward if he wants to make the practice squad. Dane Key – Unchanged: Likely was a long shot to make the team from the beginning and hasn’t really done much to help himself thus far, it seems. Cam Ross – Slightly up: Ross saw some return work on special teams and had a chunk play on an end around. He showed some potential and has a shot to make the practice squad. Kolbe Katsis – Slightly up: He made some plays during camp but didn’t do much vs. the Falcons. He has some speed and return ability, so I am going slightly up, but I had hoped for a little bit more. Joseph Manjack IV: Stock up: Manjack was second on the team in receiving yards with 3 catches for 40 yards and showed good chemistry with third-string quarterback Sam Ehlinger. If he can block and play special teams, he could make a push for a spot on the practice squad. Kyrese Rowan – Unchanged: He’s a camp/preseason body needed due to injuries. Kyre Duplessis – Unchanged: He’s a camp/preseason body needed due to injuries. Tight End Adam Trautman – Stock up: He’s a Sean Payton guy and the Broncos’ starting tight end, so his stock is and always will be up until proven otherwise. Evan Engram – Unchanged: You could go slightly up here, but I don’t think much has changed with Engram. He will be their main pass catcher at the position, but the upside seems to remain fairly limited. Justin Joly – Stock slightly down: I haven’t seen or heard many updates on Justin Joly throughout camp, and he didn’t do much in the preseason opener, so he’s slightly down for…

title: Jonah Coleman gives the Broncos another reason to be excited
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! So that Jonah Coleman is fun to watch, eh? Yes, it’s the preseason and the first game against what seems like a bad Atlanta Falcons team. But in his first NFL game, the rookie running back from Washington put on quite the display. Coleman showed what he’s been flashing in training […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - AUGUST 14: Jonah Coleman (20) of the Denver Broncos runs with the football during the Friday evening NFL preseason football game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Denver Broncos on August 14, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! So that Jonah Coleman is fun to watch, eh? Yes, it’s the preseason and the first game against what seems like a bad Atlanta Falcons team. But in his first NFL game, the rookie running back from Washington put on quite the display. Coleman showed what he’s been flashing in training camp. A strong runner between the tackles with good vision and patience. On top of that, he can pass block. The one aspect of Coleman’s game we really didn’t see on Friday is pass-catching, but that will come. When asked for his impressions of Coleman, Broncos head coach Sean Payton said to the media after the game: “Just what we’ve been seeing, right? And then you see enough of it, and you’re like, all right. Look, he’s had a good camp, and I liked his balance coming out of some of the tackles. I thought overall, the group had a good night.” vision remains a strong suit for Jonah Coleman pic.twitter.com/KRnOzoS7WA — Nate Tice (@Nate_Tice) August 15, 2026 Coleman obviously makes the Denver offense better. But more importantly, he makes the running back room better. The triumvirate of Coleman, J.K. Dobbins, and RJ Harvey has the potential to be dangerous. There’s the health issue, especially for Dobbins, in all of this. But if the Broncos consistently and effectively run the ball this season, the offense will be even harder to defend. Plus, it’ll make Bo Nix and the passing game even better. The fact that Coleman carried over what he’s been doing in training camp to the first preseason game is a positive development. Now, if the rookie can continue to build on this and stay consistent, he’s going to play a big role in this offense and in the success the Broncos expect this season. Horse tracks

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp observations, Day 13: Tate Ratledge gets work at center
summary: The Detroit Lions were back in pads on Sunday, slowly ramping things back up in their 13th training camp practice of the 2026 preseason. A couple of unexpected absences popped up at Sunday’s practice, but we also saw some injured players return, like Juice Scruggs and Derrick Moore. The pair took to the field in […]
full_text: Detroit Lions guard Tate Ratledge (69) practices during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions were back in pads on Sunday, slowly ramping things back up in their 13th training camp practice of the 2026 preseason. A couple of unexpected absences popped up at Sunday’s practice , but we also saw some injured players return, like Juice Scruggs and Derrick Moore. The pair took to the field in pads for the first time as they continue to build back up after soft-tissue injuries. Juice Scruggs and Tate Ratledge split reps at center; IOL shuffle Because this was Scruggs’ first practice in pads, the Lions appear like they want to keep his acclimation tempered a bit. He started most “team” series—save the final few—but at the halfway point, Scruggs went to the sidelines. That decision let the offensive line adjust its interior combination and test other options. When Scruggs exited, Tate Ratledge stepped in at center with Christian Mahogany shifting from left to right guard to accommodate for Ben Bartch at left guard. With this combination, they could see where Ratledge is at in his development at center, make room for Bartch to get reps with the first team, and give Mahogany some looks from the right side. The difference between the two combinations was drastic. When Scruggs was at center, the offensive line looked solid, but when they shifted to Ratledge inside, they appeared more vulnerable to blitzes, and Ratledge botched at least two snaps. While the second combination arguably puts the Lions’ five most talented linemen on the field at the same time, the cohesion was clearly absent, illustrating how important it is to find the “right” combination and “fit.” Jahmyr Gibbs’ dynamic in passing game Gibbs has shown off his running skills since returning to the field after his holdout, but on Sunday, his pass-catching prowess was on display. During one-on-ones, Gibbs worked in with the wide receivers, and then found himself on the positive end of several catches on the day. His best came during the first offensive rep of an “unscripted” series, when he ran a wheel route against Derrick Barnes for an easy 20+ yard touchdown. Once Gibbs got the angle on Barnes, he cleared him in an instant and then his speed took over, presenting a large target for Jared Goff to drop the pass into. This part of Gibbs’ game looks like it will be a weapon for offensive coordinator Drew Petzing this season. Tay Martin continues to show up in multiple ways In the battle amongst the reserves, Tay Martin continues to make a name for himself. “Tay Martin showed up again, blocking, made a one-on-one catch, separated, special teams,” coach Dan Campbell said of Martin’s performance against the Bengals last Thursday. “He forced a penalty, and that was just one play on special teams. He made more than that.” On Sunday, with Jameson Williams absent, Martin and Tom Kennedy rotated in JAMO’s spot with the first team. When the kick coverage units took the field, Martin was once again with the special teams starters, and then on punt coverage, Martin was part of the top four at the gunner position, working with Keith Abney on the second unit. “It was great to get out there with the ones,” Martin said after practice. “To get a chance to go against the ‘one’ defense, get some reps with Jared, it’s a great opportunity for me.” When the conversation turned to special teams, Martin noted that his experience playing defensive back has given him an advanatge—similar to what we see with Sione Vaki. “My whole life I played DB, safety and corner,” Martin continued. “So that gave me a physical edge because on ’teams,’ you’ve got to be physical. Each play is about who wants it more. You need a whole lot of effort to be where you need to be.” Aidan Hutchinson dominates, Derrick Moore shows range We don’t always talk about the superstars in observations because the best players in this league typically don’t surprise; they just play great every day. However, today was an exceptional day for Hutchinson, even by his standards. Hutchinson opened the 11-on-11 drills with two sacks in the first three plays. On the second, he collapsed the left side of the line, driving his blocker (not sure if it was Penei Sewell because of my angle of the play, but it would make sense based on where Hutchinson lined up) all the way back to Goff, creating a massive pileup of bodies that drew a big reaction from the crowd. Hutchinson continued to be disruptive when matching up against Blake Miller, routinely forcing the rookie to work at every step. Eventually, Hutchinson would get his third sack of the day, putting an end to the first-team final series of practice. While Hutchinson had a monster day, fellow edge rusher Derrick Moore showed well in his first padded practice in the NFL. While he didn’t register a sack, he did find ways to create pressure from the rush end position. But even more impressive was when the Lions shifted Moore to a stand-up, pass-rushing linebacker role, which allowed him the range to roam and threaten interior gaps. It’s a new wrinkle for the rookie, but also something we suggested the Lions might consider given his college tape at Michigan. Linebacker blitzes resulting in pressures Speaking of linebackers, we saw a lot of variance from them in this practice. Beyond shifting Moore to linebacker for a few reps, we also saw dual SAM linebackers, double A-Gap blitzes, and pressure throughout the day. Derrick Barnes took advantage of Ratledge’s first rep at center, forcing a quick pressure with an A-Gap blitz. Later, he got another pressure during red zone drills. Erick Hunter also found a lot of daylight when he blitzed the A-Gap and was in clean for a sack. Then, in the final drill of the day, the Lions sent a lot of pressure at Luke Altmyer, and while Sione Vaki consistently picked up the blitzing linebacker, it opened up windows for the edge rushers to get home. NB competition down to Christian Izien and Keith Abney The Lions have seen as many as four players taking first-team reps at nickel corner throughout camp, but over the past week, the competition looks to be narrowing down to Christian Izien and rookie Keith Abney. On Sunday, both rotated through reps with the starters, while Ennis Rakestraw and Roger McCreary have only been taking reps at outside cornerback. This competition is far from over, and both look in great spots to make the 53-man roster, but the Lions appear to be keeping their options wide open in this position battle. Quick hitters: TeSlaa continues to work through a rough patch, but on a fourth-down play during an “unscripted” series for the first team, Jared Goff delivered a 24-yard jump ball for him in the end zone, and TeSlaa elevated over Ennsis Rakestraw and Thomas Harper for a wonderful contested touchdown catch . Priestly continues to get emergency reps in OL/DL run drills and made two notable plays that opened big holes, one alongside Mahogany and another on a pull. Skyler Gill-Howard and Ahmed Hassanein continue their momentum from the preseason. Both stood out in “run fits” drills, and then combined for a pressure/sack during 11’s. By the end of practice, each got some rotational work with the first team. Ben Stille has a tough path to make the 53-man roster, but he routinely makes plays (including pressures and sacks) in practice, and it feels like it may only be a matter of time before he gets more reps. Greg Dortch made a veteran returner play during special teams drills, fielding a kick near the sidelines, but making sure to put his foot out of bounds before catching the ball, which would have resulted in the offense getting the ball on the 40-yard line. Anthony Lucas closed out the day with a bang. In the final unscripted series for the second team, Lucas registered two pressures and a sack in a wildly impressive performance.

title: Detroit Lions waive 2 injured players, add new cornerback
summary: Prior to their Sunday training camp practice, the Detroit Lions made a couple of transactions. As previously reported, the Lions signed running back Trayveon Williams. However, they also signed cornerback Ekow Boye-Doe. In order to make room for both players, the Lions waived both Kye Robichaux and safety Loren Strickland with injury designations. Robichaux (broken […]
full_text: LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - MAY 16: Ekow Boye-Doe #28 of the DC Defenders catches a football in warmups ahead of the game against the Louisville Kings at Lynn Family Stadium on May 16, 2026 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images Prior to their Sunday training camp practice, the Detroit Lions made a couple of transactions. As previously reported, the Lions signed running back Trayveon Williams . However, they also signed cornerback Ekow Boye-Doe. In order to make room for both players, the Lions waived both Kye Robichaux and safety Loren Strickland with injury designations. Robichaux (broken foot) and Strickland (lower body) suffered their injuries in Thursday’s preseason game. They will now head to waivers, and assuming no one signs them in the following 24 hours, both will revert back to Detroit’s injured/reserve list. If they stay there, their seasons are over. However, Detroit could opt to give both players an injury settlement payout, which would give them an opportunity to rejoin the team later in 2026. As for the new cornerback, Boye-Doe is coming off a short stint in the UFL. With the DC Defenders, he played in nine games, logged 142 defensive snaps, earned a 74.9 PFF grade, and was credited with four pass breakups. He was also active on special teams, logging an additional 138 snaps on that unit. Prior to the UFL, Boye-Doe spent time with the Chiefs, Giants, and Cardinals. He only made six game appearances in the NFL, all in 2023 as a rookie in Kansas City. He played 13 defensive snaps and 84 special teams snaps that year. At 6-foot, 177 pounds, Boye-Doe is tall but slim for the cornerback position. The Lions are relatively crowded at the cornerback position with Rock Ya-Sin, D.J. Reed, Ennis Rakestraw, Nick Whiteside, Roger McCreary, and Khalil Dorsey. That said, Whiteside missed Sunday’s practice, and the Lions may want more depth to play in the upcoming preseason games. However, Boye-Doe will have to catch on quick to make an impression. Roster cuts day is less than two weeks away (Aug. 30).

title: Detroit Lions injury updates: Jameson Williams absent Sunday
summary: The Detroit Lions donned the pads again on Sunday as they ramp training camp practice up now that the preseason opener is well in the rear-view mirror. There were a couple new absences from practice on Sunday, but we don’t necessarily have a ton of information on those situations—particularly with starting wide receiver Jameson Williams. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) practices during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions donned the pads again on Sunday as they ramp training camp practice up now that the preseason opener is well in the rear-view mirror. There were a couple new absences from practice on Sunday, but we don’t necessarily have a ton of information on those situations—particularly with starting wide receiver Jameson Williams. Here’s everything we currently know about the injury situations. Note: These injury notes are based on our observations, as there is no official injury report this time of year. Returned to practice: TE Jackson Meeks (undisclosed) OT Devin Cochran (undisclosed) After an unexplained absence on Saturday, Meeks was back in the lineup and did not appear to have any limitations. Cochran was suited up and went through some individual drills, but by the end of practice he was back in street clothes, not participating in any team drills. He’s still working his way back from an undisclosed injury. Limited practice: C Juice Scruggs (soft tissue) Scruggs got his first padded work on Sunday with the first team offense. However, about halfway through each drive he played, he swapped with Tate Ratledge, who slid over from right guard to center. Then it was Christian Mahogany who kicked over to right guard and Ben Bartch filling in at left guard. This appears to be the Lions just managing Scruggs’ workload while starting to dip Ratledge’s toe in at center. Seth McLaughlin was exclusively with the second and third teams. Not practicing: RB Isiah Pacheco (knee) RB Jacob Saylors (ankle) WR Jameson Williams (undisclosed) OT Giovanni Manu (NFI) C Cade Mays (wrist) EDGE Payton Turner (back) DT Mekhi Wingo (concussion?) DT Myles Adams (undisclosed) LB Damone Clark (undisclosed) LB Jimmy Rolder (leg) CB Nick Whiteside (undisclosed) S Kerby Joseph (PUP, knee) S Brian Branch (PUP, Achilles) There is no public information on why both Williams and Whiteside were missing from Sunday’s practice. During Saturday’s practice, there was no observed moment where either player suffered an injury, but we’ll see what their status is on Monday. Dan Campbell also has a press conference scheduled for Monday afternoon, so we’ll hopefully get an update then. Filling in for Williams was both Tom Kennedy and Tay Martin, who shared first-team reps. With D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin as the first-team cornerbacks, it was mostly Ennis Rakestraw and Khalil Dorsey with the second team, with some Roger McCreary mixed in. Myles Adams was working with a trainer during Saturday’s practice, so his absence on Sunday is not a surprise.

title: Dan Campbell speaks on Seattle Seahawks agreeing to sign Terrion Arnold
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have reportedly agreed to sign former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold. The signing is not yet official, as the franchise is still working out details with the league on the timing and viability of the signing, while Arnold continues through the legal process involving eight felony charges from an incident in Florida […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold (6) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Tuesday, July 22, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Seattle Seahawks have reportedly agreed to sign former Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold. The signing is not yet official, as the franchise is still working out details with the league on the timing and viability of the signing , while Arnold continues through the legal process involving eight felony charges from an incident in Florida earlier this year. “We have an agreement with him, and we’ll see,” Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said. “But I just really don’t know how we’re going to do it.” On Sunday, Lions coach Dan Campbell was asked about the league’s interest in Arnold following Detroit’s decision to cut him shortly after the first-round cornerback was arrested in June. Campbell was completely understanding that several teams—reportedly at least eight—were doing their research on Arnold. “No, I’m not surprised. Every team is going to do their due diligence,” Campbell said. “So it’s like we would if we were in their seat, like Seattle or New York or whatever; we would’ve done the same thing. Let’s see what we can find out, whatever we can. Arnold was selected by the Lions in the first round of the 2024 NFL Draft, 24th overall. While his career never budded in Detroit, there were flashes that he would reach his full potential. As defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard put it a few weeks ago, Arnold “had number one cornerback potential, but it was still untapped.” Campbell continues to praise both Arnold’s play and his character, despite the team’s decision to part ways with him. “We know that him coming out, he’s a good kid, he’s got ability, he’s got all of these—we’ve seen them on tape,” Campbell said. “So, no, I’m not surprised by that. Look, I have no ill will whatsoever toward Terrion. I wish him the best. And I wish everything and everyone the best in that whole situation. That’s the best way to put it.” Detroit has opted to move on without the need to add someone to replace Arnold’s spot on the roster. D.J. Reed and Rock Ya-Sin have assumed the starting roles in training camp, with Ennis Rakestraw and Nick Whiteside appearing to be the primary backups.

title: The overlooked Detroit Lion who just ‘does everything right’
summary: The life of a nose tackle is an unheralded one. They don’t typically accumulate a ton of box score statistics. Their job is often to take up space and free up other players to make plays. And, on a very basic level, the amount of punishment you take eating double teams from 300-pound players seems […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive tackle Chris Smith (90) practices during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The life of a nose tackle is an unheralded one. They don’t typically accumulate a ton of box score statistics. Their job is often to take up space and free up other players to make plays. And, on a very basic level, the amount of punishment you take eating double teams from 300-pound players seems miserable. And the players who take that relentless punishment and play at the highest of levels rarely get any national praise. Two of the best nose tackles in recent history—DJ Reader and Damon “Snacks” Harrison—have a total of ZERO Pro Bowls and one All-Pro nod between them. For the past three seasons, nose tackle Chris Smith has quietly sat on the Lions’ roster. A Michigan native, Smith entered the NFL as an undrafted player, and he’s only made five game appearances for Detroit since they signed him in 2023. But he has also essentially never left the building. Sure, there were times he was cut, signed to the practice squad, and cut again. But Detroit has always seemingly found a way to bring him back. And last year, he made the team’s 53-man roster for the first time out of training camp. The Lions keep finding room for Smith, simply because he keeps doing everything they ask of him. “He just does everything right,” coach Dan Campbell said on Saturday. “He does all the little things right. He doesn’t make the same mistake twice. He’s the guy you love to coach because he’s up here all offseason, works his tail off, is always trying to hone his game. He plays disciplined football.” During Thursday night’s preseason opener against the Cincinnati Bengals, you’d hardly notice Smith unless you were going out of your way to watch him. He logged a single tackle on his 29 defensive snaps, and PFF gave him a paltry 47.3 grade. But he was the first person who jumped out in the film upon Campbell’s re-watch of the game, and it was one particular moment that quintessentially defined the kind of player Smith is. In the second quarter, the Bengals had the ball first-and-goal from the Lions’ 7-yard line. Smith substituted in, but noticed that there wasn’t another defensive tackle who came in with him. That left him without a linemate and Detroit without an 11th player. While Smith would normally play the 1-tech—lining up opposite the center’s shoulder—he instinctively slid into the 0-tech, heads up with the center. That evened out the line, and he knew he now had to take on all three interior offensive linemen. “He’s smart enough to say, ‘You know what? Fine.’ He just gets to a zero nose to balance out the front,” Campbell said. “We only got three. And he battles in there. He takes three guys on.” That kind of attitude defines who Smith is as a person. When he talks about the thankless nature of his job, he simply states: “That’s what I signed up for.” For him, he gets satisfaction when he opens opportunities for others. “That’s the job, making sure the linebackers are kinda untouched, and I try to do my best for that for the guys behind me so they can go and play fast, too,” Smith said. “It’s really just part of the job. You’re in the middle of the defense, that’s your job is to close it up.” Much like his play, Smith isn’t loud when he talks, but he gets the message through. He’s never had the boisterous personality of a cocky cornerback or the neediness of a diva receiver. So in a lot of ways, this job is perfect for him. “I think just my personality, too. I’m not really a camera guy or anything like that,” Smith said. “It comes a little easier for me.” In Detroit’s culture of gritty work, doing your job, and lifting up your teammates, Smith is the perfect fit. “He plays discipline football. He’s a grinder, man. He’ll do it. He’ll take on double teams for 60 plays if you ask him to do it,” Campbell said. “And that’s a thankless job, and it’s hard, and it’s nobody really sees that. You don’t get any love. But he doesn’t care. To him, that means more to him to know that he’s keeping his linebacker free like that’s his heaven. So, it’s unselfish, and it’s hard. It’s a nasty job, and it’s not for everybody. And so that’s why you appreciate it.” And while he may not be getting the outside love from analysts and fans who often overlook the importance of a nose tackle, he is getting plenty of praise and encouragement from inside the building, and that could mean locking up another spot on the 53-man roster this year. “Coach Campbell and the (other) coaches, they see that. The linebackers see that,” Smith said. “So that’s kinda where some of the praise comes in.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: 4 key advanced stats from Detroit Lions’ preseason opener
summary: The Detroit Lions kicked off their preseason slate with a wet—and often sloppy—60 minutes of football on Thursday night against the Cincinnati Bengals in Ohio. While the weather made it harder to come to definitive conclusions about the play on the field, particularly at some of the skill positions, there’s still plenty to review and […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - AUGUST 13: Keith Abney II #28 of the Detroit Lions celebrates recovering a fumble with teammates during the second quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions kicked off their preseason slate with a wet—and often sloppy—60 minutes of football on Thursday night against the Cincinnati Bengals in Ohio. While the weather made it harder to come to definitive conclusions about the play on the field, particularly at some of the skill positions, there’s still plenty to review and consider from the first bit of preseason action. As we’ll do every week throughout the season for this Lions team, we have some data we can comb through courtesy of Pro Football Focus that better helps us understand the football the Lions have played thus far—and what to look forward to in the coming weeks. Let’s take a closer look at the Lions by the numbers after their loss to the Bucs. Pro Football Focus’ premium statistics are an invaluable data point for football fans to better understand the game. Consider subscribing to PFF to have full access to a plethora of stats and grades to keep you informed about the NFL—and college football, too. Also, NFL Pro is supplying some innovative and illustrative advanced statistics of their own that are worth checking out for the price of admission . 16.7 pass-rush productivity After a long and winding road back to the football field, Ahmed Hassanein returned and made the biggest impact on the defensive side of the ball last night. Dan Campbell may have manifested Hassanein’s sack of Joe Burrow , but it was the second-year edge rusher who stunted and drove his way to making it a reality. Ahmed got 'em! pic.twitter.com/qLYfqIXgVr — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 13, 2026 Through the first seven games of the NFL’s preseason, Hassanein’s 16.7 pass-rush productivity score via PFF is the second-highest score amongst 117 qualifying defenders (minimum nine pass-rushing snaps). He recorded five total pressures on 21 pass-rushing snaps, including 2.0 sacks and a forced fumble against the Bengals. 82.1 and 81.9 run-defense grades Being a cornerback for the Lions ain’t easy. Detroit puts a lot of responsibility on their respective plates, and one non-negotiable is their attitude and aptitude in run defense. Two cornerbacks in Detroit’s secondary graded out exceptionally well in run defense against the Bengals on Thursday evening: Roger McCreary (82.1) and rookie Keith Abney (81.9) . McCreary has reportedly had a relatively quiet camp after many expected him to be the team’s starting nickel cornerback, but his 12.5% run-stop rate was tied for the third-best mark among 79 qualifying cornerbacks (minimum five run-defense snaps). If McCreary continues to look impressive in run defense—and in coverage where he earned an 86.3 coverage grade, allowing zero completions on two targets—he’ll move his way off the bubble and firmly onto the team’s 53-man roster. As for Abney, it’s an encouraging sign to see his plus-run defense show up as soon as his first taste of NFL competition. Detroit has had to rely on their depth heavily at cornerback the last few seasons, and if Abney can continue to stack performances like his first game, the Lions could feel more comfortable should they need to break the glass in case of emergency. 6.38 yards after contact per attempt Jacob Saylors, on a down-to-down basis, seemed to have the most impactful play amongst the players on offense, and Dan Campbell agreed after the game. “He was probably our most potent player on offense, Campbell said of Saylors in his post-game press conference. ”He made a lot of plays for us. He’s a steady workhorse.” Ok Saylors! pic.twitter.com/1ocIid6dzy — Detroit Lions (@Lions) August 14, 2026 Beyond his sick throwback running back aesthetic, Saylors’ play matched his look. He was efficient and effective as both a runner and a receiver, rushing for 6.9 yards per carry (55 rushing yards total) and posting 9.3 yards per reception (28 receiving yards total). But on a night where Detroit’s offensive line was clearly still getting its footing, especially in the ground game, Saylors earned every yard: of his 55 rushing yards, 51 of those yards came after contact, and Saylors averaged a whopping 6.38 yards after contact per attempt—good for second among 23 qualifying running backs in Week 1. 28.3 coverage grade On the Lions’ third defensive series, Ennis Rakestraw’s night played out in a nutshell. A nice pass breakup on first-and-10 from Rakestraw quickly gave way to the worst series of events. He allowed a 20-yard reception on third-and-16 [ note: Campbell put the blame on a different defender for this play ], an 11-yard reception on second-and-20, and an 8-yard reception on third-and-9. After giving up three straight completions for a total of 39 yards, Rakestraw’s awkward angle of attack on a tackle attempt three plays later injured him and put him out of play for the rest of the game. In total, Rakestraw surrendered four catches on five targets for 44 yards and earned a 28.3 coverage grade from PFF, the second-worst grade out of 104 qualifying secondary players so far through Week 1 of the preseason. The good news is that Rakestraw avoided a major injury, but the concerning news for the third-year player is that he has roughly two weeks to prove reliable and capable as a defender to justify his spot on the roster.

title: Discussion: Who should be the Detroit Lions’ starting 5 offensive linemen?
summary: Early in training camp, coach Dan Campbell expressed some urgency in settling on a starting offensive line for the 2026 season, so the unit could build some chemistry going into the regular season. “As fast as we can get them and the secondary to work together. You know, ‘Okay, these are the guys,’ now we […]
full_text: From left, Detroit Lions guard Miles Frazier (71), offensive lineman Larry Borom (79), and tackle Blake Miller (76) practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, July 29, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Early in training camp, coach Dan Campbell expressed some urgency in settling on a starting offensive line for the 2026 season, so the unit could build some chemistry going into the regular season. “As fast as we can get them and the secondary to work together. You know, ‘Okay, these are the guys,’ now we need them to work together and get as many reps as we can. So, look, we’re trying to figure this out as fast as we can,” Campbell said on Day 1 of training camp. Unfortunately, the Lions were thrown a couple of curveballs. Potential starting left guards Christian Mahogany and Ben Bartch both missed a significant amount of practice early in camp. Then, Detroit was dealt a blow last week with starting center Cade Mays suffering a broken wrist, which will likely sideline him for at least two months. On top of that, backup center Juice Scruggs missed about a week of practice, too. Detroit seems to have settled on three positions: left tackle (Penei Sewell), right guard (Tate Ratledge), and right tackle (Blake Miller). But the other two spots remain up for grabs. So today’s Question of the Day is: What should the Lions’ starting offensive line look like? My answer: Don’t overcomplicate things. The starting lineup should be the most common starters we’ve seen at each position this camp among the healthy players. That means: LT: Sewell LG: Mahogany C: Scruggs RG: Ratledge RT: Miller I thought Mahogany had a better preseason game than many gave him credit for. It seemed his down-to-down performance was overshadowed by two penalties. Campbell gave Mahogany plenty of credit for what he put on tape. “I thought he was a physical force,” Campbell said. “And when he does it right, it’s pretty, and it’s powerful. It’s explosive. And in the pass game he’s got anchor. And then sometimes it just gets a little out of sorts. So, it’s just the consistency of it.” Now, Campbell did also say the left guard position will remain a competition, whether it be Ben Bartch or even Juice Scruggs nipping at Mahogany’s heels. Still, I think Mahogany remains the man for the job because it’s tough to even trust Bartch to stay healthy, and I think Scruggs’ best position is at center. Which leads me to the center competition. I thought Seth McLaughlin’s Lions preseason debut was somewhat encouraging. Sure, there were lapses and some mental errors (that should probably be expected given the mash-up offensive line they started on Thursday), but there were a lot of really solid reps he put on tape, as well. “He’s quick. He’s super sharp, and he’s quick, and he’s really good at the second level,” Campbell said of McLaughlin. “And then pass game is the anchor. He’s just got to bend. […] I thought he did that the other night. I did think he anchored better. I thought he strained. I thought he tried to do all the little things and that’s a credit to him. So, I certainly was not disappointed with him the other day.” Still, I think Scruggs is the guy. He’s more experienced at the position, having made eight starts for the Texans at center and producing an average PFF score during those reps . McLaughlin should certainly be given every chance to compete for the job, but I have Scruggs as the favorite, especially considering he took first-team reps on Saturday upon his return from injury. What is your preferred offensive line starting combination? Share your thoughts in the comment section below. Join the conversation! title: Aaron Banks did not have knee surgery
summary: On Friday, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur was asked directly whether or not projected starting left guard Aaron Banks, who started training camp on the physically unable to perform list with a knee injury but has since been activated to the roster, had surgery this offseason. LaFleur’s response? “I’ll let him answer that.” […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 27: Aaron Banks #65 of the Green Bay Packers lines up before a play during an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on November 27, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Friday, Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur was asked directly whether or not projected starting left guard Aaron Banks, who started training camp on the physically unable to perform list with a knee injury but has since been activated to the roster, had surgery this offseason. LaFleur’s response? “I’ll let him answer that.” Banks, while on the active roster, has only been participating in individual drills for the Packers lately, not team drills, which has led to Jacob Monk and Jager Burton earning some extra playing time with the first-team offense. Banks also didn’t suit up for the team’s preseason opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday, with Monk and Burton starting at guard. After practice on Sunday, the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel ’s Tom Silverstein got to the bottom of the surgery question with Banks. According to Silverstein, Banks did not have surgery, and Banks stated, “Nobody’s more frustrated than I am about not being able to be out there right now.” Apparently, Banks’ knee injury started during offseason workouts, and he has claimed that he’s dealing with tendinitis “that flared up anytime he does strenuous football movements.” Per Silverstein’s report, Banks believes he will recover by the start of the regular season, and that surgery is not an option the team has suggested. In other injury news, tight end Tucker Kraft, who got into team periods for the first time all training camp after returning from an ACL tear, told the press after practice that he believes that he’ll be on a pitch count until about midway through the season .
