title: On the QB1 Decision and Takeaways from the Vikings’ 1st Preseason Game
summary: For this article, I decided to offer (yet another) take on the Minnesota Vikings quarterback issue – delayed so it wouldn’t get lost in the shuffle – and some quick takes on the team’s first preseason game of the season. KYLER MURRAY IS OUR QB1 Kevin O’Connell made it official: Kyler Murray will be the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 15: Quarterback Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings sets up to throw 21a pass during preseason game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on August 15, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Mike Coppola/Getty Images) | Getty Images For this article, I decided to offer (yet another) take on the Minnesota Vikings quarterback issue – delayed so it wouldn’t get lost in the shuffle – and some quick takes on the team’s first preseason game of the season. KYLER MURRAY IS OUR QB1 Kevin O’Connell made it official: Kyler Murray will be the starting quarterback . Oddsmakers and betting markets had the implied probability in the 85-90% range since Murray signed here, so it’s not surprising. Let’s talk it over. While no one was officially named the starter earlier in the offseason, it was widely understood that it was Murray’s job to lose and J.J. McCarthy’s job to win. That’s an important distinction, and it put the lion’s share of the pressure on McCarthy’s shoulders. He not only had to outperform Murray, but also do so consistently, day in and day out, from the start of training camp. That didn’t happen. While he had his good days, the benefits of spending two years in KOC’s system and the stated offseason goals of improving his mechanics and footwork did not translate into performances that approached that level. Another layer to this discussion, which took a back seat to the day-to-day hot takes on the QB battle, is that KOC needs not only a double-digit win season to improve on 2025 but also that elusive playoff win. As ESPN’s Kevin Seifert noted , there are only three NFL head coaches since 2000 who have reached a sixth season without a playoff win: Washington’s Jay Gruden (2014-18), Houston’s Gary Kubiak (2006-10) and Cincinnati’s Marvin Lewis (2003-07). KOC doesn’t want to be the fourth. Would a 10-7 or 11-6 season and another one-and-done in the playoffs cost him his job? Possibly, but I’d say it’s unlikely. Would his seat become very warm in 2027? Definitely. Kyler Murray is simply the safer bet, and, given the history, I’d say he’s a strong favorite to match or surpass Sam Darnold’s performance. The DN’s Warren Ludford broke it down earlier and noted that Murray was able to match, and in some cases exceed, what Darnold did with an inferior Arizona Cardinals team in 2024. Now, as the known starter, Murray’s consensus fantasy numbers for 2026 are around 3,500–3,600 passing yards, 23.5–24.5 TDs, along with 480–500 rushing yards and 3.4–3.7 TDs. That would be nearly 1,000 passing yards and over 10 passing TDs less than Darnold had in 2024. And we’ve added Jauan Jennings. Yeah, if he stays healthy, which is not an unserious concern given the past five seasons, those projections will be the absolute floor. J.J. MCCARTHY’S FUTURE At this point, there’s nothing new to say about it that hasn’t already been said. I’m not going to rehash or revisit my views on J.J. McCarthy. If you care to, you can read them here , here , here , and elsewhere in my DN entries. I’m a huge admirer of the guy, and I still think he can be an NFL starting quarterback. I believe he is more the player in the Cowboys/Lions away games last year than in the Packers road game. But the simple fact is that he no longer controls his own destiny with the Minnesota Vikings. For him to see the field in 2026, it will be because of an injury or poor performance by Murray, or even by Carson Wentz. Yes, we are at that point (more on that below). He’s under contract through next season, but again, either the Vikings or Murray would have to opt for a change for him to get back into the QBOTF discussion. At this point, I know only two things: First, I’m officially done drafting and developing the QBOTF thing for the foreseeable future. It’s been 21 years since Daunte Culpepper threw his last pass in a Vikings uniform. At this point, I’m all-in on the free-agent/veteran reclamation strategy. If the Super Bowl win ever comes, it’ll be that way. It is what it is. Do I like it? Nope. But there’s that well-cited definition of insanity. Second, if McCarthy is traded or moves on after 2027 and becomes a successful NFL quarterback for the L.A. Chargers, Rams, or elsewhere, I’m going to lose it. Of all the awful things that have happened to Vikings fans over the decades, watching McCarthy lead another team to a Super Bowl would be near the top. And if he actually won one? Don’t even go there. It would be an extinction-level event for the collective psyche of Vikings fans. PRESEASON GAME #1 IN THE BOOKS The Vikings defeated the New York Giants 13-10 to win the season’s first preseason game . The major story of the day was that newly signed safety/linebacker Jamal Adams was carted off the field with an apparent non-contact leg injury. The worst-case scenario is expected. Adams made an excellent play for a TFL early in the game, exploding through the line to make a play. The potential of what could’ve been was an early bright spot. But, alas, like Chad Greenway in 2006 and Phil Loadholt in 2015, the Vikings will likely lose a valuable contributor for the season before the games count for real. Wishing Jamal Adams all the best and a quick recovery. I’ll leave this here: pic.twitter.com/QGHi0UwTzL — Eric Thompson (@eric_j_thompson) August 15, 2026 Some other quick thoughts: Kyler Murray was fine. In his one series, Murray hit a difficult out route to Jordan Addison on 3rd and 8 for a key first down during a 10-play, 54-yard opening drive that ended in a field goal. QB2 competition discussion has arrived. J.J. McCarthy never found a groove in his limited snaps. He did hit Myles Price on a nice gain under duress, but overall it was largely uneventful. Carson Wentz got more action than intended due to an injury to Max Brosmer and finished with a 103.6 QB rating and a nice TD pass to Myles Price (more on that in a moment). Wentz looked more comfortable in the offense, and it’s worth watching to see whether it was an anomaly or the new reality. The run game was excellent. The first few series showed what this run game can be this year. Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason rushed six times for 44 yards (7.3 yards per attempt). Demond Claiborne played well, carrying momentum from a strong training camp to date. Myles Price gets the game ball. Price was excellent, catching four passes for 51 yards (12.8 yards per catch), including a gorgeous one-handed touchdown grab from Wentz. Price was a lock for the team due to his special teams prowess, but he may be working his way into seeing some not inconsequential reps as a WR this season. Dallas Turner: So far, so good. Turner’s ongoing development – especially in the context of the Jonathan Greenard trade – was high on this Vikings fan’s radar during training camp and preseason. If today was any indication, things are going splendidly. Not only did he record a sack in limited snaps, but he was also all over the place and seemed near the ball on every play he was in. Jacob Thomas’ strong training camp continues. The undrafted free agent from James Madison built on the momentum of an impressive training camp with a nice interception. Given the unfortunate Adams injury, Thomas could find himself in the mix more than anticipated from this point forward. We’ve made it, folks. Competitive football is finally back for the Minnesota Vikings!

title: 6 performances of note from the Patriots’ 16th training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots turned back the intensity on Sunday. After a full pads session on Saturday and another expected to come on Monday, head coach Mike Vrabel opted for a walkthrough. To recap it, please head over to our Patriots training camp notebook. In the meantime, here is who caught our eyes. Standout of […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 3: New England Patriots running back Lan Larison and cornerback Channing Canada talk during training camp on August 3, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The New England Patriots turned back the intensity on Sunday. After a full pads session on Saturday and another expected to come on Monday, head coach Mike Vrabel opted for a walkthrough. To recap it, please head over to our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eyes. Standout of the day N/A: Considering that the Patriots held a walkthrough on Sunday, we will refrain from naming one individual player as today’s standout. The day was not about performance and competition, after all, but more on mental work and — from our point of view — who was part of which groups. Other performances of note RB Lan Larison and RB Jam Miller: Larison was with the starting offensive group on Sunday working with quarterback Drake Maye as the No. 3 running back. He additionally also served as part of the top kickoff returner pairing alongside Kyle Williams. Miller, meanwhile, seemingly remains behind him on the depth chart for both roles despite a solid showing in the preseason opener. TE Tanner Arkin: Despite seeing consistent starter reps earlier in camp, Arkin did not join Drake Maye and company in the practice bubble on Sunday. He stayed outdoors with the backups providing looks for the starting defense, while only Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon went indoors. DT Isaiah Iton: With Christian Barmore still absent, Iton was the fourth defensive tackle to run with the top-level unit of Milton Williams, Cory Durden and Joshua Farmer. The Rutgers product was a dark-horse roster candidate last summer already, and could be in the process of becoming the same in 2026. ED Quintayvious Hutchins: The seventh-round rookie found himself among the first-team edges on Sunday. His group also included Dre’Mont Jones, who was back after exiting Saturday’s practice, as well as Gabe Jacas and Elijah Ponder. Maybe it’s a sign of things to come for the youngster, who has had some solid moments this summer. S John Saunders Jr: Coming off a good week that saw him catch an interception in both the joint practice with the Colts and the subsequent preseason game, Saunders Jr. was given reps with the starting defense on Sunday. He served as a fourth safety behind Kevin Byard, Craig Woodson and Dell Pettus. The Patriots will be back on Monday for another session closed to the general public. As always, Pats Pulpit will have you covered and bring you updates straight from Foxborough.

title: Patriots training camp recap: Offense preps for Seattle’s environment
summary: The New England Patriots were back on the practice fields for the second straight day on Sunday but dialed down the intensity to a walkthrough session. Here’s what went down on the back practice fields. Setting Attire: Jerseys and shorts Duration: ca. 90 minutes (10:00 a.m.-11:30 p.m. ET) Conditions: Sunny, temperatures in the mid 80s It was a […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 06: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel arrives to New England Patriots training camp on August 6, 2026 at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots were back on the practice fields for the second straight day on Sunday but dialed down the intensity to a walkthrough session. Here’s what went down on the back practice fields. Setting Attire: Jerseys and shorts Duration: ca. 90 minutes (10:00 a.m.-11:30 p.m. ET) Conditions: Sunny, temperatures in the mid 80s It was a light day for the Patriots as they worked at a walkthrough pace, although still used the time productively on Sunday. Attendance Absent: CB Christian Gonzalez, OLB Xavier Holmes, OL Ben Brown, WR Kyle Dixon, DL Christian Barmore Returnee: OLB Dre’Mont Jones, WR Kobe Prentice, DB Eric Butler, LB Chad Muma PUP/NFI: ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler While New England saw a handful of players remain absent — continue to be highlighted by Christian Gonzalez — several players did return to the practice fields. That included top outside linebacker Dre’Mont Jones, who left practice early on Saturday due to a cut on his finger. Takeaways Silent count: Near the end of practice the Patriots top offense and scout team defense departed the practice field and moved inside the bubble with head coach Mike Vrabel. With the music then turned up, the offense’s communication was stressed as they worked on their silent count. “This is our second or third time doing it. One of those things that works well for away games,” Mike Onwenu said. “Working on the silent count and being in those uncomfortable situations.” The Patriots worked silent count at times last season, but Onwenu noted that work has transitioned into the bubble this year to be “more ahead of it this year.” Part of that may be due to an expected noisy environment Week 1 in Seattle. Saunders’ reward: Second-year safety John Saunders was a part of the Patriots first team defense as work split between two fields. He rotated in with Dell Pettus behind Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard. Saunders has had an impressive start to the summer with a pair of interceptions on the practice field and one in Thursday’s preseason opener. His play appears to have him climbing the depth chart, potentially jumping veteran Mike Brown. After joining the Patriots in the middle of last season, Saunders has noted his comfort level has risen getting more experience in the system this summer. “It feels amazing now — second year with the guys and coaches,” he said. Offensive lines: To no surprise, the Patriots top offensive line remained the same with Will Campbell, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, Mike Onwenu, and Morgan Moses aligning from left-to-right. The second unit has seen movement the last two days after losing top interior backups Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich (IR) in the preseason opener. On Sunday, that line featured: Marcus Bryant, Mehki Butler, Jacob Rizy, James Hudson, and Caleb Lomu from left-to-right. Other notes: As work split between two fields, the top seven wide receivers stayed to work with Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito. Will Campbell shared the left arm brace he has been wearing is precautionary. With Christian Barmore continuing to be sidelined, Isaiah Iton saw time with the first-team defense. Iton has impressed this summer and looks primed for a practice squad spot on a deep defensive line. Quintayvious Hutchins spent time with the first-team defense along the edge. Kyle Williams and Lan Larison repped as the top kick return pairing. Efton Chism and Jam Miller were the second unit. Gabe Jacas was the last player off the field working late on pass rush moves with Iton and Khalil Jacobs. Preview The Patriots will be back at it on Monday where the intensity is set to ramp back up. A busy week then continues with the Philadelphia Eagles coming to town for a pair of joint practices on Wednesday and Thursday.
author: Brian Hines

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Evaluating top rookies in preseason debut
summary: The New England Patriots’ preseason is fully underway following their opener against the Indianapolis Colts. Work now transitions back to the practice fields where intensity will pick up with a pair of joint practices against the Philadelphia Eagles. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots offensive tackle Caleb Lomu (74) warms up with linebacker Gabe Jacas (50) before a game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots’ preseason is fully underway following their opener against the Indianapolis Colts. Work now transitions back to the practice fields where intensity will pick up with a pair of joint practices against the Philadelphia Eagles. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Rookie debuts With Drake Maye and the Patriots regulars sidelined in the team’s preseason debut, New England’s younger players received the bulk of the reps. That meant extensive action for their first three draft picks: Caleb Lomu, Gabe Jacas, and Eli Raridon. Here’s how they fared: OT Caleb Lomu: The Patriots first rounder played all 39 of his snaps at right tackle Thursday night. New England didn’t ask him to handle many traditional drop backs in the passing game as the game plan featured plenty of quick games and chip help. Lomu looked mostly comfortable in those situations and a did not allow a pressure in the passing game. As a run blocker, his athleticism was seen during a fourth-down conversion but the rookie struggled at times moving defenders. OLB Gabe Jacas: It was also a mix of good and bad for Jacas, who was challenged by Vrabel on special teams during the game. Jacas showed his power on numerous occasions in the run game while also pushed a defender into Anthony Richardson’s lap on an early interception. The outside linebacker was a bit too aggressive at times which led to big plays in the option and screen game, but more experience should benefit him in those situations. “Keep coaching and keep working with Gabe, knowing that some of those things that’ll translate from special teams have to translate to defense, and we try to explain to him that whatever it was in the joint practice, it’s going to be faster in the game. Things happen quicker,” Vrabel said. TE Eli Raridon: The box score was measly for Raridon as he finished with just one catch on four targets for eight yards. But, a 24-yard gain off of a catch in the flat (a staple for Raridon this summer) that showcased his athleticism was negated due to Lomu being illegally downfield. Raridon then had a great block working to the second level on New England’s longest run of the night. As for the rest of his night as a blocker, Raridon often got in the way but didn’t seem to generate much push. “I mean, we want to move him as far as we can possibly move him. I thought it was okay,” Vrabel said. “I think he continues to improve blocking and he’s willing, and so that’s the one thing that I really think I’ve been pleasantly surprised with, just his willingness to do that.“ Resetting the market The Seattle Seahawks made Devon Witherspoon the richest cornerback in NFL history on Saturday inking the star to a four-year, $132 million contract — a deal that may now serve as an outline for Christian Gonzalez, who shares an agent with Witherspoon. Witherspoon’s $33 million average clears Denzel Ward’s $31.1 million, while his $101 million guaranteed is also the most by any cornerback in NFL history: Witherspoon: $101 million guaranteed Trent McDuffie: $100 million (signed this offseason) Derek Stingley: $89 million (signed last offseason) Sauce Gardner: $85.6 million (signed last offseason) Sweet dreams Kyle Williams showcased his impressive release package throughout his rookie year. That was on display in Thursday’s preseason opener on multiple occasions — including his 12-yard touchdown where he easily beat Jonathan Edwards off the line of scrimmage. Williams has watched wide receivers like Davante Adams, Keenan Allen, Doug Baldwin, Stevie Johnson, etc. to hone his craft, which he finds himself thinking about often. “I have dreams about releases,” Williams said. “It’s something that I just do in my sleep.” Receiver snaps With A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, and DeMario Douglas not playing in the preseason opener, the Patriots opened the night with Kayshon Boutte and Mack Hollins out wide. The duo played 16 and 13 snaps, respectively, as they worked in with Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III before ceding the way to players further down the depth chart. Boutte’s playing time was notable as he remains uncertain about his Patriots future, while his lack of a target across three drives could also highlight why he requested a trade back in the spring as he looks for more volume in a contract year. The Colts, who got a look at Boutte in Tuesday’s joint practice and in the preseason opener, remain active in the wide receiver market as Alec Pierce remains sidelined with an ankle injury. Chism’s role As Mike Vrabel stated, Efton Chism III found a role on the football team last year and made it easy for the Patriots to keep him around. This summer, that role has seemingly expanded. Chism has worked in with the first-team offense at both the Z and slot positions — even sharing the field with DeMario Douglas at times — and has often been called upon in run situations and in the red zone. “I think he’s got a good skill set of being able to get in there and block, but also marry some of that with some of the run action passes,” Vrabel explained. “He competes. He always takes care of the guy. He protects the guy with the ball the best that he can, and I always see him looking to finish when he does not have the football in his hands, and continues to make big plays and show up when we need him.” Virtual help The Patriots’ new New Balance Athletics Center features a virtual room that each position room opens into. Inside is a 20-yard turf field painted with lines that is the standard width of an NFL field. Virtual screens at the front of the room can then simulate looks from the classroom. Carlton Davis, who returned to practice on Saturday, was a frequent visitor in the room the last few weeks as he was sidelined with a hamstring injury that he suffered on July 28. “It’s always good to have the technology to be able to keep up with what’s going on and get the virtual learning going on,” he said. Practicing hard John Saunders signed to New England’s practice squad midway through last season on Nov. 19. Upon his arrival, the Patriots’ practice intensity surprised the rookie, which led to a message from his head coach three weeks into his tenure: practice harder. The safety took the advice in stride and eventually needed to be told to “dial it back a little bit,” as Saunders joked he was trying to cause havoc on the practice fields. But the 24-year-old has continued to practice hard this summer, which has led to a pair of interceptions and another one in Thursday’s preseason opener. “It feels amazing now — second year with the guys, the coaches,” said Saunders. “And they know how to teach here. So, it’s amazing to just learn from them and just continue to build each and every day.” Week ahead The Patriots will remain busy on the practice fields this upcoming week with multiple joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles before taking on the Birds in their second preseason game. From an install standpoint, Mike Vrabel noted this will be an important week. “This will be a big week for us,” he said. I think we talked yesterday about where we’re at, the list of stuff that we like, that we don’t like, that we would still like to investigate a little bit. title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Jaguars
summary: The New Orleans Saints dropped their first game of the preseason to the Jacksonville Jagaurs in a 24-20 loss. Despite dropping a 20-6 lead, the loss wasn’t all bad for New Orleans. As depth pieces begin to make more plays, the Saints roster will begin to fill out closer to the regular season. These are […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 15: Zach Wilson #4 of the New Orleans Saints throws a pass during the third quarter of the preseason game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Caesars Superdome on August 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Morgan Simmons/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints dropped their first game of the preseason to the Jacksonville Jagaurs in a 24-20 loss. Despite dropping a 20-6 lead, the loss wasn’t all bad for New Orleans. As depth pieces begin to make more plays, the Saints roster will begin to fill out closer to the regular season. These are the players who bettered their chances to be on the final 53, while other stock fell in the loss. Up: QB Zach Wilson Quarterback Zach Wilson was the team’s best passer in their Week 1 preseason loss. Wilson finished the day completing 11-of-16 passes for 145 yards and a touchdown. The former second-overall pick finished the game without a turnover and taking just one sack. Wilson’s passing efficiency is what stands out, averaging 9.1 yards an attempt. In his 16 attempts, Wilson passed for more yards than Spencer Rattler and Hunter Dekkers combined, and was the only quarterback to end with day with a passing touchdown. Wilson’s passes were quick and put into spots where only his receivers could get them. Some throws really stood out, with Wilson putting some heat on it, drilling it to his target in tightly contested coverage. If there wasn’t a QB2 competition before, Wilson’s strong day definitely opened the door. Up: EDGE Michael Heldman EDGE rusher Michael Heldman was the game MVP, racking up an astonishing 2 sacks, 3 tackles for loss, and 3 QB hits in his limited snaps. Heldman and Garret Nelson were a handful for the Jaguars tackles, and Heldman came out the day with a stat line that guarantees him consideration for the final roster. Heldman went undrafted despite an impressive 9.88 RAS score combined with a 10.5 sack season in 2025. Many wondered why the former Central Michigan pass rusher wasn’t drafted, but it appears the Saints got a gem on the theird hands after his impressive NFL debut. Up: CB Martin Emerson Jr. Entering the season, cornerback was a huge question, but it appears the Saints have their picks for starters going into Week 1 as Kool-Aid McKinstry and Quincy Riley each didn’t play. McKinstry is the team’s surefire CB1, but there are major concerns at CB2. After New Orleans signed Martin Emerson Jr, many questioned if Riley would remain the starter after earning that role last season. Despite what appears to be a safety net for the second-year cornerback, Emerson had a strong day on Saturday, logging 3 pass deflections and almost came away with an interception. Emerson offers experience to the Saints secondary while still just 25-years-old. With some more strong preseason performances, the former Cleveland Browns cornerback could see more playtime in the regular season. Down: K Charlie Smyth The kicking competition through camp has been bumpy. Each kicker has had their good and bad days, and consistency remains a concern. On saturday, Tanner Brown went 2/2 on field goal attempts, with a long of 49. Charlie Smyth wasn’t as fortunate, missing his lone attempt from 52 yards. A 52-yard field goal isn’t an easy feat, but missing after bumpy training camp showings puts Smyth’s position on the team in question. Down: QB Spencer Rattler Rattler’s biggest issues that led to his benching was his lack of big play ability. Saturday’s loss only emphasized this, with the third-year quarterback logging 42 passing yards on the day. Rattler’s 3.8 yards per attempt was the lowest among the Saints’ three passers. With Wilson’s strong performance, Rattler’s QB2 chances took a significant hit. He hasn’t shown the ability to create plays, and the touchdown drive he took part of was thanks to a 82-yard kick off return and a 9-yard run from Audric Estime just one play after. Rattler’s name has come up quite a bit recently as a trade candidate for the Saints. Many question the team’s reasoning for a possible trade, with Ratler being a solid back up otpion at quarterback. But more strong performances from Wilson and a lack to prove himself by Rattler could result in him being part of another team in the near future.

title: Game Recap: Saints host Jaguars to open preseason
summary: The New Orleans Saints kicked off the 2026 preseason on Saturday night as they hosted the Jacksonville Jaguars in the Caesars Superdome. Here’s a quick recap of all the action from the black and gold’s only home game before the regular season. First Quarter Things got off to a flyer for the home team, as […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 15: Zach Wilson #4 of the New Orleans Saints against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Caesars Superdome on August 15, 2026 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints kicked off the 2026 preseason on Saturday night as they hosted the Jacksonville Jaguars in the Caesars Superdome. Here’s a quick recap of all the action from the black and gold’s only home game before the regular season. First Quarter Things got off to a flyer for the home team, as Ty Chandler returned the opening kickoff for 86 yards to set up Audric Estime for a 9-yard touchdown run and an instant 7-0 Saints lead. Nick Mullens started the game at quarterback for Jacksonville and led a decent opening drive for the visitors, with a 17-yard throw to rookie wideout Josh Cameron helping the Jaguars into the red zone. But Mullens was intercepted by Jaylan Ford, keeping the visitors scoreless. The teams proceeded to exchange three straight 3-and-outs, the last of which ended in a muffed punt by Ryan Wright that gave the Jags a short field. They capitalized on the opportunity with a 54-yard field goal from Cam Little to get them on the board. Saints quarterback Spencer Rattler fumbled on the opening play of the ensuing drive, and the Jags once again took advantage of a short field with another field goal to put the score at 7-6. Second Quarter Rattler was better as the Saints offense returned to the field, finding a variety of receivers on a 15-play drive. The hosts failed to convert a 3rd-and-long, but Tanner Brown converted his 49-yard field goal attempt to extend the Saints lead. The team traded quick punts once again before Carter Bradley, in at QB for Jacksonville, was intercepted by Jayden Price. Zach Wilson led the Saints offense back onto the field and thought he’d thrown a touchdown to Bub Means on the first play of the drive. But Means was ruled just short of the end zone, and tight end Oscar Delp caught the short touchdown pass from Wilson instead to put the Saints up 17-6. Jacksonville proceeded to punt once again, and Wilson wasted no time in the 2-minute drill. He found Bub Means for 37 yards, and Barion Brown for 28 yards as the Saints quickly moved into field goal range. Brown converted again from 29 yards as the Saints brought a 20-6 lead into the half. Third Quarter Bradley returned to deliver his best drive of the day for the Jags, who drove 79 yards in just over 6 minutes to open the half. Hunter Long caught a 1-yard touchdown, and J’Mari Taylor ran in a 2-point conversion attempt to bring the score to 20-14. Wilson connected with Jalen Moreno-Cropper for 14 yards as the Saints drove to set up another field goal attempt. But Charlie Smyth missed wide right from 52 yards. The Jags offense returned to the field, and Bradley converted a 3rd-and-18 with a pass to Brady Boyd to extend the drive into the fourth quarter. Fourth Quarter A holding penalty paused momentum for Jacksonville as they drove into Saints territory, and they had to settle for a 36-yard field goal. But the Saints went 3-and-out as Hunter Dekkers entered the game at quarterback, giving the Jags the ball and a chance to take the lead, trailing just 20-17. And Joey Aguilar did just that as he entered the game at QB, finding Trebor Pena for 43 yards to set up a 2-yard touchdown run from J’Mari Taylor. The extra point gave the Jags a 24-20 lead. Both teams proceeded to punt in quick succession, leaving the Saints 2 minutes to find a winning touchdown. Dekkers almost found the score the Saints needed, with big gains to Moren0-Cropper and Trey Palmer helping the black and gold into the red zone. But the final play of the game was an incomplete pass intended for Moreno-Cropper in the end zone, and the Jags held on for the win. The Saints head to Los Angeles to face the Rams on Saturday, before the trip to Dallas to close out the preseason.

The 28-year-old Webb has played in 36 NFL […]
full_text: Sam Webb with the Cleveland Browns. | Getty Images Cornerback Sam Webb has retired from football four days after signing with the New York Giants. Webb signed with the Giants on Thursday, played 14 snaps on Saturday in the Giants’ preseason game against the Minnesota Vikings, and was placed on the NFL reserve/retired list on Sunday. The 28-year-old Webb has played in 36 NFL games over four seasons with the Las Vegas Raiders, Carolina Panthers, and Cleveland Browns. The Giants have had a rash of injuries at cornerback, with Dru Phillips, Paulson Adebo, and Greg Newsome all missing time. With this news, the Giants will likely be back in the cornerback market. The Giants might also be looking for running back help after the news that Dante Miller could miss time with what coach John Harbaugh believes is a groin or soft tissue injury. The Giants will practice at Quest Diagnostics Training Center Monday and Tuesday before traveling to Miami on Wednesday for Thursday’s joint practice against the Miami Dolphins.

full_text: Dante Miller | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect New York Giants running back Dante Miller could miss time with an injury suffered Saturday against the Minnesota Vikings. “We might have a situation with Turbo (running back Dante Miller),” head coach John Harbaugh said on Sunday. “We’ll see with a soft-tissue going type thing, we’ll see how that turns out today.” Miller, 27, spent the last two seasons on the Giants’ practice squad. He was active for two games last season, but did not get a carry or pass reception. Miller appeared to be injured covering a punt in the second half of Saturday’s game. He did return to action, but was clearly uncomfortable in the locker room afterwards. Miller appeared to have only an outside chance to make the roster, with Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary seemingly locked into spots. Missing time could be the death knell for his roster chances. Miller carried five times on Saturday for 14 yards (2.8 yards per carry), returned three kickoffs for a 23.0-yard average, and made a tackle after quarterback Brandon Allen threw an interception.

title: Giants vs. Vikings: Rookie report — who played well, and who did not
summary: We finally got a look at the New York Giants 2026 draft class in a live game setting. The Giants’ rookies played early and often in their first NFL action, with each of the Giants first four picks starting against the Minnesota Vikings. The Giants want to build through the draft, so these young men […]
full_text: New York Giants linebacker Arvell Reese before a play. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We finally got a look at the New York Giants 2026 draft class in a live game setting. The Giants’ rookies played early and often in their first NFL action, with each of the Giants first four picks starting against the Minnesota Vikings. The Giants want to build through the draft, so these young men will be their future as well as a big part of their present. And while the Giants lost the game — and go into the next week of practice with plenty of things to work on — there were also plenty of encouraging signs in their individual play. Arvell Reese (LB) The Giants’ first draft pick started the game and played 16 snaps, notching two total tackles. Reese was largely as advertised in the draft and in practice reports. He plays with an impressive downhill trigger, quickly closing on running plays. Reese plays very fast, with an accurate first move as well as his twitchy athleticism allowing him to fly to the ball. He also arrives with bad intentions and hits like an absolute truck. We’ve seen the clips of his tackle in the run game, but instead I want to highlight Reese taking on the Vikings’ fullback. He quickly diagnoses the play, knifes into the gap, and blows up the lead blocker, forcing the running back to cut back. The run goes for 4 yards, but that isn’t Reese’s fault. ( I’d place the blame on DL Josh Toupu, who doesn’t stay square to his blocker and gives up a massive hole on the right C gap. ) He’s surprisingly fluid in space, which should give Dennard Wilson plenty of options for simulated pressures or zone blitzes. It’s going to be fun to watch Reese develop and see how he’s employed as we see more of Dennard Wilson’s defense. Francis Mauigoa (G) Mauigoa got quite a bit of work against the Vikings, playing 32 offensive snaps (as well as 1 special teams on the extra point attempt), or almost half of the offense’s 67 total plays. Mauigoa played with both Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston. Mauigoa is clearly a massive, powerful young man. He’s able to distort the line of scrimmage going downhill as a run blocker, both in man-gap and zone schemes. He also clearly understands how to use angles to his advantage, creating creases even when he can’t drive defenders off the ball. We don’t know for sure if Mauigoa will ever move outside to tackle, he does have very good feet for a guard, easily mirroring interior rushers in pass protection. He lunged a bit on some of his blocks, which he’ll need to clean up to avoid being on the ground too much. However, his hand usage was solid and he’s strong enough to be a problem even without perfect technique. Mauigoa absolutely looked like he belonged as a guard on an NFL offensive line, though after the game he said that he doesn’t just want to belong, he wants to dominate. “I do honestly feel like I belong,” he said after the game. “But at the same time, I just don’t want to belong. I want to dominate the league. That’s the mentality that every kid has. As a rookie, you want to come in and you want to earn that trust.” Colton Hood (CB) The Giants’ second-round pick started the game opposite Deonte Banks and was on the field for 31 snaps. Hood was credited with 3 tackles and no passes defensed, though he may have gotten one if John Harbaugh had won his challenge. Hood played the left cornerback position, likely putting him in direct competition (or as the planned backup for) Paulson Adebo, who has historically been a LCB. Hood is a smooth mover in space with quick solid recovery quickness. He did a good job of closing when targeted in zone coverage and gave a good effort to disrupt the catch. Early descriptions of him as a “press man bully” were accurate on the field, and Hood is both very physical with his jams as well as when he’s taking on blocks. He still needs development in the technique department, but the “want to” is there. Ultimately, Hood was largely invisible and it was a bit of a surprise to see him on the field for 31 snaps (including some special teams work). That’s not a bad outcome for a rookie cornerback. Malachi Fields (WR) Fields was, in many ways, the star of the offense for the Giants. He was on the field for 21 of the Giant’s 67 offensive plays (as well as five special teams plays), but had some of the most memorable on offense. Fields plays faster than he timed at the Scouting Combine, however he’s still more of a “quicker than fast” receiver. He’s somewhat plodding unless he can open his stride, but he does have impressive short-area quickness for a big receiver. Fields also clearly understands how to use his massive catch radius, playing with excellent ball skills and strong hands. Notably, the Giants made an effort to get Fields involved as a blocker. He was occasionally put in motion before the snap and brought to the play-side. He definitely understands how to use his size against defensive backs and blocked with good competitive toughness as well. That isn’t as flashy as a scramble drill touchdown, but it’s important to the down-to-down operation of the offense. “He loves the game, he competes through the whistle,” quarterback axson Dart said after the game. “You see that in the way that not only he runs his routes but also the way that he blocks, so I think he’s just been doing what he’s been doing and I have a ton of faith in him.” Bobby Jamison-Travis (iDL) Jamison-Travis got on the field pretty early in the game, playing the first of his 27 snaps with 10:21 remaining in the second quarter. That could mean that the coaching staff is eyeing him for a move up the depth chart and wanted to see him against some of the Vikings’ better players. While Jamison-Travis didn’t record any stats in the box score, he had a good game. He’s stout at the nose tackle position (either at the 1-technique or 0-technique), and consistently created traffic jams in the middle. He’s quicker than expected in a short area, and pretty consistently rocked the center back or stonewalled double teams. Jamison-Travis also played with an mpressive motor for a big man. He won’t be running many people down, but he consistently disengaged and hustled to the play, even if there was no hope that he’d make the tackle. J.C. Davis (OT) Davis didn’t get onto the field with the offense until about halfway through the third quarter (7:57 remaining), playing left tackle with the third team. The results were decidedly mixed. On the plus side, he does show good play strength once engaged with good pad level, and was able to wall off rushers when they met him head-on. Likewise, he has good power and can move defenders when blocking downhill. He has smooth feet and can move laterally when he needs to. On the other hand, there were enough snaps where Davis struggled to justify concern about him. He showed a tendency to lunge into contact, as well as pivot too early and get perpendicular to the line of scrimmage instead of staying parallel. In either case, doing so created easy lanes into the backfield. That might be due to the fact that while his feet are smooth, he doesn’t look particularly quick. Davis might have more of a future as an interior lineman than as an offensive tackle. Jack Kelly (LB) The Giants’ coaching staff clearly wanted to take a long look at Kelly and had him on the field for 51 total snaps between defense and special teams. He started the game covering the opening kick-off and got on the field the first time with the defense with 13:26 remaining in the second quarter, while some starters were still on the field. Kelly was extremely active on defense and looked comfortable playing the run as well as dropping into zone coverage. Likewise, he’s explosive coming downhill as a pass rusher and had a couple nice blitzes through the interior gaps. That said, he does need to work on his technique taking on blocks. He wasn’t consistently getting his pads down when taking on offensive linemen and wasn’t really using his hands as a…

title: ‘Things I think’: Odell Beckham’s future, Jaxson Dart, and some problems exposed
summary: The New York Giants’ first preseason game, a 13-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, has given us a lot to discuss. Here are some of the ‘things I think’ after Saturday’s game. Odell Beckham’s future remains uncertain The nostalgia of Odell Beckham Jr.’s return to MetLife Stadium as a Giant was nice. Beckham got a […]
full_text: Odell Beckham | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants’ first preseason game, a 13-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, has given us a lot to discuss. Here are some of the ‘things I think’ after Saturday’s game. Odell Beckham’s future remains uncertain The nostalgia of Odell Beckham Jr.’s return to MetLife Stadium as a Giant was nice. Beckham got a couple of nice ovations from the crowd on Saturday, such as it was in a sparsely attended preseason game. That’s cool. But the nostalgia is over. Now, Beckham’s comeback after a year away from football is only about whether he can make the Giants’ season-opening 53-man roster. It’s a good question without an obvious answer. Beckham entered Saturday’s game with less than six minutes left in the first half. He played 16 snaps. He caught two passes for a measly 6 yards on Saturday. Some will point out there was a play on which Beckham was open but did not get the ball. I have heard and read the same all summer from some of my media cohorts. To me, “open, but …” doesn’t matter. The tape will tell the decision-makers what they need to know. What matters in the end is if Beckham can be among the three or four best wide receivers on the roster. If he isn’t, his path to making the roster is more difficult. NFL teams need the final player or two on the roster at positions like wide receiver to be core special teams contributors. Beckham has never been that, and won’t be now. Head coach John Harbaugh, the man who has to make the ultimate keep-or-cut decision, certainly did not guarantee Beckham a roster spot on Saturday. “I love Odell. I do. What he’s doing, what he’s fighting for, I don’t know how it’s going to turn out. It’s going to turn out the way it turns out, based on what happens,” Harbaugh said. “But to see his fight, his determination, his humility. He’s got his son in camp the other day, he’s doing it for his son. That just, as a friend, that makes me really proud of him.” Beckham is “grateful” for the chance. “Just being able to be back on the field, it truly means a lot to me,” Beckham said after the game. “I’m walking the fine line between being grateful just to be here, but still hungry and have desires to do more.” When he felt he had broken open on a deep route, he thought, “God, you’re not going to bless me like that today … I thought for a second it was about time to get back in that end zone.” But the ball didn’t come. “I felt good. I feel good being out there,” Beckham said. “I feel when you see the tape or at practice, I’m getting open. But at the end of the day, a receiver, I always talk about this, it’s the most selfless position on the field. You wait around all game for everybody to do their job just for five opportunities maybe. So when they do come their way, you’ve got to make the most of them. Today it was light, so we’ll see what happens.” What will happen is still a question without a clear answer. Jaxson Dart and the blue tent The Giants’ quarterback did not like being sent to the medical tent for a concussion check after taking a huge hit from Minnesota safety Jay Ward on Saturday. Doing so, though, was the right call by whoever made it, whether that was the on-field officials or the upstairs medical spotters. Dart, who said he had the wind knocked out of him by the hit, lay on the field for several nerve-wracking seconds before getting to his feet. Checking him was the right decision. Playing starters was the right call Except for veteran players like Brian Burns, D.J. Reader, Tremaine Edmunds, Shelby Harris, and Andrew Thomas, healthy starters played a couple of series on Saturday. I asked Harbaugh what they got out of playing: “They got reps in a game, which they’re not going to get until the first game if you don’t play them in the preseason. It’s different,” Harbaugh said. “They [the Vikings] played their whole starting defense. We played about half our starting defense to start the game. So, I decided not to play some of those starting defensive guys for that reason. I thought that they would benefit more from not playing. They played their whole starting defense. I think we played all of our starting offense, except for our left tackle, and I felt like he didn’t need it. He would be fine. “But felt like the other guys playing together was important, especially with Jaxson out there. And our quarterback got two – got, I don’t know, 10, 15 plays out there of good football. So, he’s going to be that much better for the regular season than he would have been if he hadn’t played those games. And we got out of it healthy. So, it worked.” Playing starters was the right call. The Giants are, mostly, a young team with a young, developing quarterback that is learning new schemes on both offense and defense. The offense, in particular, remains a work in progress. Dart, having survived the big hit he took, clearly needed and benefited from the live reps. “I thought it was really good,” Dart said. “I really feel like if we were on the same page, all of us, on the first drive, we would’ve scored the first drive. “It’s good for us to have those moments where we’re able to come off the field and communicate with each other to make sure that those things don’t happen again in a situation that’s outside of practice, where maybe in practice, it may be the consequence isn’t the same as in a game. So, us being able to see that, have that understanding; and then the second drive, it was just a resilient drive by us and as a whole unit, which I was really proud of.” The mess at cornerback Whether you were for or against the Giants signing Terrion Arnold , Saturday’s game provided a clear indication of the issues the Giants have at cornerback. Of course, Paulson Adebo, Dru Phillips, and Greg Newsome, the presumptive starters, did not play. Adebo, though, has not had a good training camp. Newsome is coming off a couple of rocky seasons, and whether he can be depended upon is debatable. We saw a lot of rookie Colton Hood and former first-round pick Deonte Banks on Saturday. Both played 26 first-half snaps. I would call their work “uneven.” Banks, who had done good work all spring and summer while trying to resuscitate his career, committed two penalties. He did show some willingness to tackle, which was missing last season, but to my eyes did not play like a starting cornerback. Hood has shown his talent, but has also shown he has things to learn, all spring and summer. He gave up completions both times he was targeted and committed a penalty. He could have a bright future, but might not be ready to be an NFL starter just yet. So, yes, there are good reasons why the Giants should be looking for cornerback help. No ties in the preseason Rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada made a 62-yard field goal during practice a few days ago. With fourth-and-13 at the Vikings’ 44-yard line and 2:29 remaining in a game the Giants trailed 13-10, the Giants were in position to let Zvada try one in a game. Harbaugh chose to punt. I wanted to see the kid try one. Help wanted — needed — on the defensive line Reader and Shelby Harris, the veteran players who will be counted on to anchor the Giants’ run defense from their interior defensive line spots this season, did not play. That exposed the Giants’ lack of depth on the defensive line. The Giants signed a number of defensive linemen this offseason after having to trade Dexter Lawrence. They had to. The question, though, beyond Reader and Harris, has been how many of those guys are actually players you want in a defensive line rotation. After Saturday, I’m not sure how many of those players answered that question in the affirmative. The Giants gave up 5.2 yards per rush (12 carries, 62 yards), including runs of 18, 17, and 15 yards in the first half. They seemed unable to hold the point of attack. Nose tackle Josh Tupou played 21 snaps and, without the benefit of having looked at the All-22, I would say he showed why he was a practice squad player for the…

title: Eagles News: Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru offer intrigue in NFL debuts
summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles preseason: Backup QB race goes backward, Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru debut – The AthleticInternational players steal the show. When I remember this game a decade from now — what does it say about me that I might remember this game a decade from […]
full_text: Jun 10, 2026; Philadelphia, PA, USA; Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Uar Bernard (93) during minicamp at Jefferson Health Training Complex. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Eagles preseason: Backup QB race goes backward, Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru debut – The Athletic International players steal the show. When I remember this game a decade from now — what does it say about me that I might remember this game a decade from now? — I’ll focus less on the offense and the backup quarterbacks and more on an otherwise unremarkable drive in the third quarter when Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru played their first snaps of football in a game — ever. “How exciting for those two guys to be playing in an NFL football game?” Sirianni asked. Bernard, a native of Nigeria, and Weru, a native of Kenya, did not start practicing football until the spring. They didn’t wear full pads until two weeks ago. Consider how many youth league, high school or college games most everyone else on the field played before their NFL debuts. Bernard and Weru did it for the first time in this setting. In the locker room after the game, teammates told Bernard how proud they were of him. “It’s a dream come true for me,” said Bernard, who had chills when he went on the field. “I think I’m proud of myself.” There were signs of major development necessary, but there were also flashes you can get behind — especially with Weru. He gets less attention than Bernard, but don’t forget about the undrafted edge rusher who was an international rugby player. He had a quarterback hit, and you saw his burst chasing down the passer. Weru is 6 feet 4 and 244 pounds with a 4.45-second 40-yard dash and 41 1/2-inch vertical leap, and he’s demonstrated in practice tools that are hard to find at the position. Both players are a work in progress. Vic Fangio said they’re “light-years away.” But Weru said this week that you need to celebrate the wins during the development process. It was a refreshing outlook. And seeing Bernard disengage a blocker or Weru apply pressure, it’s hard not to think about how far they’ve already come rather than focus on how far they still have to go. Saturday night was a benchmark for them. It will be a lasting memory from the game. Eagles lose to Ravens: Taking stock of Markel Bell, Tanner McKee, and Willie Lampkin – PHLY Stock up, Joshua Weru. It took exactly one play in an organized football game for Joshua Weru to make an impact. The 6-4, 244-pound edge rusher from Kenya registered a quarterback hit on his first play early in the third quarter and got another pressure later in the drive. Weru’s moments were mostly flashes, but that could be sufficient to garner enough attention across the league to give him a case to make the initial 53-man roster. No other team had tape on Weru before tonight, and what he showed on tape tonight shows the upside that’s been apparent for those watching closely during training camp. Eagles-Ravens preseason observations: Position battle updates, injury news, and more – BGN The Philadelphia Eagles kicked off their 2026 preseason schedule with a LOSS to the Baltimore Ravens. Final score, which doesn’t matter, but we’re logging it here anyway: 24 to 7. To no surprise, the Eagles barely played any starters in this game. You could say that any football is better than no football but this was mostly a boring game. The Eagles’ offense mustered just 100 yards on their first 31 plays before Cole Payton finally led a scoring drive later in the fourth quarter. Read on for some noteworthy moments from Saturday night. Eagles-Ravens, a Training Camp Fight, And the Jalen Hurts INT Controversy with BLG! – The Ringer’s Philly Special The Eagles opened their 2026 preseason Saturday night with a 24-7 loss to the Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore. Sheil is joined by Brandon Lee Gowtown of Bleeding Green Nation to discuss the loss and any concerns or bright spots from the game. What’s going on with the backup QB battle between Andy Dalton and Tanner McKee? Who stood out to Sheil and BLG? Plus, a look ahead to the joint practices with the Eagles and Patriots and a discussion about ice cream. Slopfest – Iggles Blitz were dominant in all three phases of the game. The Eagles were out-gained by almost 300 yards and didn’t score until the final minutes of the game. Give Baltimore credit for playing well. But also make sure to acknowledge how poorly the Eagles performed. There were some good individual showings, but the overall team struggled mightily. The Eagles were 0 for 9 on third downs. They were 10-96 with penalties. The coaches will have a lot of mistakes to point out and teach from. Too many. The bad showing doesn’t mean the Eagles are a bad team or it is time to panic. 2026 NFL preseason Week 1: Game takeaways, analysis – ESPN Eagles: The best rookie on the field for the Eagles was tackle Markel Bell, as has been the case all summer. The 6-foot-9, 346-pound third-round pick out of Miami got the start at right tackle and showed the power and poise (he drove a defensive lineman back 6 yards on one run play) that have fueled the organization’s increasing confidence in him. With Lane Johnson coming off an injury-riddled season and likely entering his last NFL campaign, Bell’s emergence appears right on time. Quarterback Cole Payton, the fifth-round pick out of North Dakota State, got the offense rolling late, using his legs to get into striking distance before throwing a TD pass to Erik Ezukanma. Philadelphia will need more patience when it comes to edge rusher Joshua Weru and defensive tackle Uar Bernard, who are products of the NFL’s International Player Program. Both made their pro debuts and held their own, all things considered. Weru even registered a QB pressure and a tackle. Eagles 53-man roster projection, after the first preseason game – PhillyVoice Quarterback (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton. The Eagles feel likely to trade either McKee or Andy Dalton, with Dalton being to more likely candidate, though Howie Roseman will have to hope nobody watched the Eagles’ first preseason game. For now, I’ll project that Roseman will be able to get that done before 53-man cutdowns. However, I also believe that he’ll be willing to keep four quarterbacks at 53-man cutdowns if he doesn’t get any trade value for either guy. Roob’s Instant Observations after a near-disastrous Eagles preseason opener – NBCSP This was about as lifeless start as you could imagine for the Sean Mannion offense. Yeah, no starters. Yeah, first preseason game. Yeah, new scheme. And yeah, Payton’s efforts in the final minutes helped them avert an embarrassing shutout. Still, you’d like to see more than this. Even with this rag-tag collection of backups, practice squadders and NFL hangers-on, this just shouldn’t happen. Not this bad. I get that you’re vanilla and I get that you don’t want to show anything. But let’s at least try to look like a real NFL offense maybe? I don’t want to get too carried away. We’re still a month away from the regular-season opener, there are joint practices with the Patriots next week and two more preseason games and obviously none of the Eagles’ starters and most key backups were watching from the sideline. But not an auspicious debut for Mannion. Eagles’ undersized center Willie Lampkin continues to impress in the preseason – PFT Lampkin is tiny by NFL offensive lineman standards — something that was pointed out on the TV broadcast of the Eagles-Ravens game — but at some point, a player’s on-field performance has to matter more than his height and weight. Even if he’s shorter than 5-foot-11 and less than 280 pounds, Lampkin belongs in the NFL. Young Eagles defender seemed like an afterthought. Now, ‘he’s gotten so much better’ – NJ.com With 8:53 remaining in the first quarter Saturday night, Eagles defensive tackle Ty Robinson exploded off the ball and…

title: Eagles vs. Ravens Preseason: The good, the bad, and the ugly
summary: The first dress rehearsal did not go well. The Eagles’ 24-7 loss to the Baltimore Ravens on Saturday at M&T Bank Stadium night honestly means nothing. What does is a new offense still under wraps. Who was playing to win and who wasn’t. So, let’s take look. The Eagles were outgained 440 yards to 159, […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - AUGUST 15: Andy Dalton #14 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts after a play against the Baltimore Ravens during the first half of the preseason game at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The first dress rehearsal did not go well. The Eagles’ 24-7 loss to the Baltimore Ravens on Saturday at M&T Bank Stadium night honestly means nothing. What does is a new offense still under wraps. Who was playing to win and who wasn’t. So, let’s take look. The Eagles were outgained 440 yards to 159, outperformed by surrendering 31 first downs to 6, and what was highly irritable—even for a game that does not count—is 10 penalties for 96 yards. It is preseason, though getting flagged 10 times for nearly 100 yards has more to do with discipline than is does strategy. The defense was so horrid it made future accountant Joe Fagnano into Joe Montana, completing 22 of 28 for 224 yards and a touchdown. Preseason or no preseason, it was difficult to watch this mess. There was a big mound of ugly, some bad and fee scant moments of good in the Eagles’ 24-7 loss to the Baltimore Ravens. The Good Linebacker Jeremiah Trotter Jr. finished with five tackles, two solo, and a sack—all in the first half. He will again make the Eagles and push for a starting role. He was a plus in what was otherwise a dismal night overall for the defense. In the time he was in the game, he was always around the ball. Defensive tackle Ty Robinson looks like he will add depth to the defensive line. By all accounts,he has had a very good training camp and ended the game with two tackles, one tackle for loss, a quarterback hit, and a sack in the first quarter, forcing a third-and-17. Running back Will Shipley looked good, rushing for 22 yards on 7 carries. Back-up quarterback Cole Payton looked the best of the three quarterbacks. He completed 4 of 9 passes for 34 yards and a touchdown, going off script and hitting Erik Ezukanma in the corner of the end zone. Rookie tight end Eli Sowers did not start well, getting flagged for holding on his first snap as an NFL player, but he did finish with 3 catches on 3 targets for 12 yards. The glaring problem is could he block? That could be a problem. Cornerback Kelee Ringo may be the only player to be both good and bad. Good: He had the only interception of the game at the Eagles’ 9 in the final minute of the first half. It was a great defensive play, closing on the play in the back end of the end zone. You can also find Ringo under bad. Wide receiver Darius Cooper led the Eagles with 2 catches for 21 yards, the longest being for 13 yards. Cooper also had a Dalton pass go through his hands in the first quarter. The Bad Not a good way to start. Rookie tight end Elie Sowers getting flagged for holding on the very first play of the game. Ringo getting called for pass interference in the first minute of the first half. He is on the bubble to begin with, although he is a very good special teams player. He was stung on the Ravens’ first touchdown. But Ringo, being Ringo, did come back to pick off a pass on the very next play that he committed the pass interference. The Eagles showed pieces of what the offense could look like. But it was not the best start for Mannion, who decided to coach the offense from the sideline. The Eagles were 0 for 9 on third-down conversions. They did not truly move the ball until the third-stringers were on the field late in the game. The Ugly Yeah, this belongs in the ugly department—the Eagles’ offense. Okay, Sean Mannion saw his offense go 0-for-9 on third-down conversions, gain a scant 81 yards of offense in the first half, and total 159 yards of total offense for the game. Everything seemed out of sync. Give Mannion points for some glimpses of play design, but otherwise, it was not a good start, regardless of who was playing. Back-up quarterback Andy Dalton was, well, horrible. He went 3-of-6 for 20 yards, averaging 3.3 yards per attempt. The Eagles failed to achieve a first down under Dalton’s watch. Dalton was supposed to be leading in the back-up quarterback spot with Tanner McKee, and did not help himself, with the Eagles running nine plays for 12 yards under Dalton. Getting flagged 10 times for 96 yards is enough to drive any coach up a wall—and it will be a point of emphasis for head coach Nick Sirianni when watching the game film this coming week.

title: Steelers training camp: Punches thrown and a clear leader for the RB3 role headline Sunday’s practice
summary: LATROBE- After a laid-back and padless Saturday practice that lasted just about 55 minutes in total, Sunday’s session was as physical and as long as we have seen any practice this camp. Practice came to sort of a natural stop after a massive fight in which the whole team got involved. Here is everything you […]
full_text: LATROBE- After a laid-back and padless Saturday practice that lasted just about 55 minutes in total, Sunday’s session was as physical and as long as we have seen any practice this camp. Practice came to sort of a natural stop after a massive fight in which the whole team got involved. Here is everything you need to know from a fun-filled Sunday practice. Punches were thrown At the very end of practice, wide receiver Max Hurleman caught a ball and ran forward for a few yards before rookie safety Robert Spears-Jennings lowered his shoulder and put Hurleman in the dirt. The receiver did not take it too kindly, as he popped right back up and got in the rookie safety’s face. Seconds later, Hurleman and Spears-Jennings seemed to take each other to the ground fighting. This prompted the entire team to run over and get involved. Somehow in the middle of it all, tight end Jaheim Bell and safety DeShon Elliott got into a serious altercation in which Bell was landing haymakers on Elliott. Bell even ripped off Elliott’s helmet at one point and was punching him in the face rather than his helmet. The huge brawl was eventually broken up by the coaching staff and some of the veteran players. The team ran one more play after the scuffle, but tempers had flared too much by that point to continue practice for much longer. This frustration seemed to be building all practice long between the offense and defense after newly signed linebacker Elandon Roberts seemed to disregard the “no live tackling” rules at several points during camp. There were plenty of moments where you could audibly hear the offense yell “come on E-Rob.” Although it wasn’t Roberts involved in the fight that boiled over, he certainly played a key role in why we saw such a big disagreement today. Lew Nichols has a strong hold on the RB3 job I do believe we are getting to the point with Lew Nichols where calling him a “camp darling” doesn’t begin to to do him justice. Despite averaging just 3.6 yards per carry in the team’s preseason opener, Nichols paced the Steelers running back room and led them in touches. In the walkthrough period to open practice, Nichols was on the field with Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle with the first and second teams while Eli Heidenreich and Kaleb Johnson were over on the second practice field with the third and fourth teams. Nichols was always the third RB in line to get touches during drills and team periods. The way things played out in the preseason game and where the team has him playing in practice suggests they are at least strongly considering Nichols for the role. The running back had several touchdowns during 11-on-11 drills in practice and clearly has the support of others on the offense. Nichols could be on the verge of making the team with a strong finish to the preseason. Rodgers-to-Wilson connection continues to pace the offense During the first play of the team’s “Franco moment,” Rodgers stepped back and fired a laser over the middle to Roman Wilson, who caught the ball in stride for a huge gain. Wilson was quiet in his limited playing time in the preseason, but continues to have one of the strongest camps of any player. Later in practice, Rodgers hit Wilson again for a huge gain on what seemed to be the same play. Wilson seems to have his most success in the slot, which should bode well for his regular season projections given he has had to play outside more with the injuries to DK Metcalf and Michael Pittman Jr. On Thursday, he mostly played outside with both Metcalf and Pittman out. Other notes: RB Eli Heidenreich made a spinning catch for a touchdown on a Mason Rudolph pass, which got a huge reaction from the crowd. The Mt. Lebanon kid is already a massive fan favorite. CB D’Shawn Jamison had a quality day with a PBU in 7-on-7’s and an interception of a Drew Allar pass in red zone drills. DL Yahya Black was disruptive today. Black blew up several run plays during team periods and looks to be set up for increased opportunities in year two. Payton Wilson seems to have improved as a run defender this camp. Today was no exception as he was in the backfield and stopped a Lew Nichols carry for what would have been a tackle for a loss in a game setting. Elandon Roberts is back in his old number 50 jersey, while Jamin Davis is now wearing 57. DeShon Elliott and Darnell Washington were chirping at each other long after a play in which Elliott broke up a pass intended for Washington. This might have played into the serious altercation Elliott later had with Bell. Let us know what you think in the comments . summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers have had a busy offseason when it comes to getting contract extensions done. After declining the fifth-year option on offensive tackle Broderick Jones, Pittsburgh signed edge rusher Nick Herbig to a four-year, $100 […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Nick Herbig #51 of the Pittsburgh Steelers looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers have had a busy offseason when it comes to getting contract extensions done. Three of their top five draft picks from their 2023 draft class have signed long-term extensions with the team. After declining the fifth-year option on offensive tackle Broderick Jones, Pittsburgh signed edge rusher Nick Herbig to a four-year, $100 million deal, followed by Darnell Washington getting a four-year, $42 million deal. And late Friday evening, Pittsburgh came to terms with defensive tackle Keeanu Benton on a four-year, $72 million extension. During Benton’s press conference after the extension, Herbig was in attendance to support his close friend. He was asked about his close relationship with his fellow former Wisconsin Badger. “We’ve been best friends since the day we met in college,” Herbig said, via Alan Saunders . “That’s like my brother.” Fighting back tears, Herbig reminisced on the long road he and Benton have traveled together. “Just everything we’ve been through together. Seeing him [get through] all the trials and hardships. Grinding and going through the mud together. Getting drafted together. Just this journey we’ve been on. Now it’s all full circle, I can’t even out it into words.” Benton and Herbig have been teammates since 2020 when Herbig arrived at Wisconsin, making this season their seventh year together. The Steelers’ 2023 class is one of the best in recent franchise history. They can complete the quartet of extensions by coming to terms with cornerback Joey Porter Jr, who is entering the final year of his rookie deal. Let us know what you think in the comments .
